# Precautions for
# PROSECUTORS,
<note>original: "Cautio Criminalis". This is the title of one of the most famous books ever written against the legal abuses of the witch trials.</note>
->❦ Or ❦<-
## ON TRIALS
## AGAINST WITCHES
<note>original: "Contra Sagas". While "saga" literally means a wise-woman or fortune teller, in this 1631 context, it refers specifically to those accused of witchcraft.</note>
### A Book.
# FOR MAGISTRATES
### of Germany, necessary in this time,
->Moreover, for<-
## Counselors, and Confessors of Princes,
->Inquisitors, Judges, Advocates, Confessors<-
->of the accused, Preachers, and for others,<-

### BY THE AUTHOR
## AN ANONYMOUS ORTHODOX THEOLOGIAN.
<note>original: "Incerto Theologo Orthod." The book was published anonymously to protect the author, Friedrich Spee von Langenfeld, a Jesuit priest who had seen the horrors of the trials firsthand as a confessor to the condemned.</note>

<summary>This is the title page of the "Cautio Criminalis," an anonymous but revolutionary 17th-century treatise arguing against the legal procedures used in witch trials. It was written by the Jesuit Friedrich Spee to warn judges and clergy about the execution of innocent people through forced confessions.</summary>

<meta>This page serves as the opening preface to the work, establishing the author's paradoxical intended audience among German legal officials regarding the prosecution of witchcraft.</meta>

# THE AUTHOR’S PREFACE.

I have dedicated this book to the Magistrates of Germany; specifically to those who are *not* going to read it, rather than to those who are. The reason is this: if the Magistrates were already so concerned that they thought they ought to read what I have written here regarding the cases of <term>witches (original: *Sagarum*)</term> <note>The term *Saga* specifically refers to a female diviner or witch in a legal context.</note>, they would already possess the very thing for which the book ought to be read—namely, care and diligence in thoroughly investigating these cases. Therefore, for them, it is not necessary to read or to draw from these pages. On the other hand, as for those who are so negligent that they are unlikely to read or care about such matters, it is absolutely essential that they read this above all else, so that from this book they may learn to be concerned and diligent. Therefore, let those read who are not going to read; and as for those who are inclined to read, they need not read at all, etc.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Nevertheless, whether someone is going to read this book or not, I would desire that there be no one who does not at least read the single final "doubt" <note>The author refers to the *Dubia*, or formal legal-theological questions, that structure the book's arguments.</note> of this book and weigh it in his own mind.

<sig>A 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: IN-</meta>

<summary>In this preface, the author uses a rhetorical paradox to argue that his book on witch trials is most needed by the very magistrates who are too indifferent to read it. He urges even the most casual reader to consider the final "doubt" presented in the work.</summary>

# A WARNING ON CRIMINAL TRIALS
## OR
## Concerning the Trials against Witches
### THE BOOK.

---

## Question I.
### Whether witches, hags, or sorcerers truly exist? <note>original: "An Sagæ striges seu malefici revera existant?" The author uses three different Latin terms for those accused of magic: "Sagas" (often used for wise women or fortune tellers), "striges" (an ancient term for owl-like night hags), and "malefici" (literally "evildoers" or those who perform harmful magic).</note>

<image-desc>Large decorative drop cap 'R' containing vine and leaf motifs.</image-desc>

**I respond**, *that although I know some have cast doubt on this matter—even Catholics and learned men whom it is not necessary to name here; and although some seem to suspect, and not without reason, that there were once times in the Church when the <term>physical gatherings of witches (original: corporalibus Sagarum conventibus)</term> were not believed in; and although, finally, I myself—while I have dealt with various people accused of this crime in prisons quite frequently and attentively (not to say inquisitively)—have more than once had my mind so entangled that I almost did not know what to believe about this matter; nevertheless, when I finally gather the sum of my perplexed thoughts,*

<meta>catchword: it</meta>

<summary>This page opens the main text of Friedrich Spee's "Cautio Criminalis," posing the fundamental question of whether witches actually exist. While acknowledging his own deep doubts and the historical skepticism of the Church, the author prepares to address the reality of the witchcraft phenomenon.</summary>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues the opening argument of Question I. On the previous page, the author (Friedrich Spee) acknowledged the doubts many have regarding the existence of witches and admitted his own confusion after visiting prisoners. This page provides his definitive—yet carefully nuanced—position on the matter, transitioning from the admission of doubt to a call for rational, charitable inquiry.</meta>

## Question I. Whether witches or sorcerers truly exist?

*I believe it must be held as certain that some sorcerers do indeed exist in the world, and that this cannot be denied without rashness and a mark of distorted judgment. Let the authors who professionally treat this subject be consulted: <note>Spee cites the "heavyweights" of 16th-century witch-hunting theory: Nicolas Rémy (Remigius), Martin Delrio (Delrius), and Jean Bodin (Bodinus). By citing them, he establishes his scholarly credentials before he begins to dismantle their legal methods.</note> Remigius, Delrius, Bodin, and others. It is not our purpose to linger here. However, as for whether there are so many witches, and whether all those women who have been burnt to ashes <note>original: "in favillas evolârunt," literally "flown off into sparks/ashes," a poetic and grim reference to the execution by fire.</note> so far were truly such; neither I, nor many other pious men with me, believe it. Nor will anyone easily persuade me to believe it, unless they wish to examine the matter with me using judgment and reason, rather than through impulse, clamor, or mere authority.*

*This is what I most earnestly pray my reader desires, through that charity which our <term>Lawgiver (original: legifer)</term> Christ so strongly wished to be kindled among his followers. If anyone has a zeal against this crime and gnashes their teeth at the sin of <term>magic (original: magia)</term>, let them restrain themselves for a moment and add knowledge and consideration to their zeal—qualities they perhaps lack. Not every impulse comes from <term>virtue (original: virtus)</term>; some come only from one's natural temperament. Virtue is moderate and modest; it loves to be instructed, and it does not fear being diminished by becoming better informed. But if we rush headlong with impulse, and because we imagine we know everything, we refuse to learn—is it any wonder if truth escapes us in many things? Come now, reader: set aside <term>prejudice (original: præjudicio)</term> and follow modestly where I lead you step-by-step by the hand. It will not be a source of regret to have considered many things slowly and carefully.*

<summary>Spee concedes that sorcery exists in theory to avoid charges of heresy, but he immediately questions the sheer number of modern executions and calls for a rational, compassionate investigation over blind zeal.</summary>

<keywords>existence of witches, judicial caution, Christian charity, Nicolas Rémy, Martin Delrio, Jean Bodin, religious zeal, legal reasoning</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the transition from the general existence of witchcraft to the specific crisis in Germany. On the previous page, the author established that while he believes sorcery exists in principle, he doubts the sheer volume of cases and the validity of recent executions. Here, he begins "Question II," addressing why Germany specifically seems to be overrun with such cases compared to other nations, pointing toward social and psychological causes rather than supernatural ones.</meta>

DOUBT II.
B 2
<meta>catchword: Do. (The first syllable of the first word on the following page, "Docent.")</meta>

# Are there more witches or sorcerers in Germany than elsewhere?

I ANSWER. *This is a question about a matter I do not know: however, I will say a few words just to pass the time <note>original: "otij eludendi causâ," literally "for the sake of eluding idleness," a modest rhetorical device where the author downplays his own expertise</note> regarding what occurs to me. Therefore, it at least seems so, and it is commonly thought that more are found in Germany than elsewhere.*

*The REASON is this.* For first of all, it is well known that throughout Germany everything is smoking with the fires <note>original: "incendiis," referring to the execution pyres of the witch trials</note> that consume this plague <note>original: "luem," a common term for the perceived infection or contagion of witchcraft</note>. This is certainly a clear argument for how widely everyone admits the infection has spread. It has reached the point that the German name has suffered no small loss of reputation among our enemies, and, as the Scripture says, we have "made our scent stink before Pharaoh and his servants." <note>A reference to Exodus 5:21. The author suggests that the sheer number of trials has made Germany a laughingstock or a horror to neighboring nations.</note>

Furthermore, we nourish this opinion about the great number of <term>witches (original: Sagarum)</term> among us based on two main points which are worthy of note.

THE FIRST is *the ignorance or superstition of the common people.* I demonstrate it thus: All <term>Natural Philosophers (original: Physici, referring to early scientists)</term> teach that even those things which occasionally stray somewhat from the common order of nature and are usually called "extraordinary"—such as a particularly heavy rain, light hail and frost, more magnificent thunder, and similar things—are caused by entirely natural means.

<summary>The author addresses the reputation of Germany as a land uniquely infested by witches, suggesting this perception is fueled by the sheer number of executions and the scientific ignorance of the common people who mistake natural weather events for magic.</summary>
<keywords>Germany, witch trials, superstition, natural philosophy, reputation, execution pyres, common people, weather phenomena</keywords>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of Question II: "Are there more witches or sorcerers in Germany than elsewhere?" On the previous page, the author noted the high frequency of executions in Germany. Here, he moves to a psychological and scientific critique, arguing that Germans are too quick to blame the supernatural for natural phenomena or medical mysteries.</meta>

### Doubt II. Are there more witches in 
# Germany?

Doctors also teach us that livestock, no less than humans, are subject to their own diseases; they explain that many new ailments often appear in humans and cattle which have not yet been sufficiently investigated even by the physicians themselves. They tell us that many wonders lie hidden in nature which, from time to time, bring themselves to light, to the great astonishment of those who are ignorant of nature's riches. Indeed, they argue that not even the most learned man of all past centuries has been able to fully grasp the whole power of nature through his investigations, and so on. 

Thus say the doctors. Yet, should anything of this sort show itself in Germany—especially among the country folk <note>original: "Paganos," which in this legal and social context refers to rural villagers or peasants rather than non-Christians</note>—if some plague should invade the livestock, or if the sky should be disturbed and rage quite violently <note>A reference to sudden, destructive storms often attributed to "weather-making" by witches</note>, or if a doctor is stumped by the nature of some new disease, or if a very old disease does not quickly yield to the medical art; in short, if anything sinister of any kind happens that is considered out of the ordinary, we are immediately led—by I know not what levity, superstition, or ignorance—to turn our minds toward <term>sorcery (original: maleficia)</term> and cast the blame upon <term>witches (original: Sagas)</term>. 

In such moments, we cry out that we hold the entire source of the matter in our hands. Then, indeed, if we see any woman who happens to be passing by, standing near, or arriving on the scene, who is doing this or that by mere chance...

<summary>The author critiques the German tendency to jump to superstitious conclusions, arguing that many events blamed on witchcraft are actually natural phenomena or medical mysteries that doctors do not yet understand.</summary>

header: [continued from previous: Are there more witches in] Germany than elsewhere?

meta: catchword: & ma- [this refers to the beginning of the next page's text]

...doing or saying anything (for necessarily certain things must have always preceded, coincided, or followed), we summon it to blame with a sinister interpretation and, such is the malice of our nature, we stir up suspicion through the entire neighborhood. Hence it is no wonder if, within a few years, a growing rumor makes us quite wealthy <note>In this context, the author likely means "wealthy" in the sheer number of accusations or the confiscated property of the accused</note>. This is especially true since neither the preachers nor the spiritual men stir themselves here; rather, they are often caught in the same fault themselves. Nor has any Magistrate been found in Germany, as far as we know, who has unsheathed his zeal against these most pestilential whisperings <note>original: "susurrationes," referring to the quiet, toxic spreading of gossip and rumors that fuel witch hunts</note>, concerning which more will be said below in Doubt 35. 

Other nations are more cautious, and it is a disgrace that we are surpassed by them in this regard. For among them, if some boy or a head of cattle wastes away from disease, if a tree is struck or the harvest suffers a calamity, if a wind causes ruin, or a locust or mouse devours the field, they trace the entire origin of the evil back to God or to nature. They do not ascribe such things to <term>sorcery (original: maleficiis)</term> unless those events are clearly reprehensible, and the learned judge them to exceed the laws of nature.

->**SECOND is the envy of that same common folk**<-

<summary>The author argues that Germans are uniquely prone to blaming witchcraft for natural disasters and illnesses, unlike other nations who look for natural causes. He blames the clergy and magistrates for failing to stop the spread of malicious rumors.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the author's exploration of Question II: why witchcraft accusations seem more prevalent in Germany than in other nations. On the previous page, he identified "envy" as the first source of these rumors; here, he links it to "malevolence" and the social dynamics of neighborly suspicion.</meta>

### Question II: Are there more witches in [Germany than elsewhere?]

**...and malevolence**, which I demonstrate in this way: there is no nation that will not admit that there are always certain individuals to whom God grants a more generous blessing in material goods. ->DOUBT V.<-

## Whether it is therefore permitted to
## form a Legal Process against "excepted"
## crimes according to one's own discretion.

**I ANSWER: It is not permitted.**

The **reason** <note>original: *Ratio*</note> is this. For although, as I have already said, these crimes are "excepted" from what human **positive laws** <note>Laws enacted by human authorities, such as statutes and codes, as opposed to natural or divine law</note> require, they are not excepted from what human reason or **natural law** <note>The inherent sense of justice and morality believed to be common to all humanity</note> prescribes. Therefore, whatever sort of Legal Process is ultimately conducted against them—whether it follows the common order of the law or falls outside of it—it is necessary that it be of such a kind that it contains nothing at all which conflicts with right reason. This is clear in itself and requires no proof: for no one would say that something is permitted if it is contrary to reason.

I offer this warning for this specific reason: because I notice that certain Judges, while they are investigating **Witches** <note>original: *Sagas*; a term for those accused of sorcery or "wise women"</note>, allow themselves more freedom than is proper, excusing all their actions by the fact that it is an **Excepted crime**. And so, if they have relied on flimsy evidence <note>original: *indicia*; legal signs or circumstances that suggest guilt but do not constitute full proof</note>, if they have exceeded moderation in **torture**, if they have been too gullible, or if they have denied the right to a defense and similar things which are abandoned by reason, they repeatedly throw this up as a shield: that the crime was "Excepted," and in Exce- <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page; the original Latin catchword is *pris*, likely leading into *priscis* or *praescriptis*</note>

DOUBT VIII. 15

B.

# How cautiously Princes and their officials ought to proceed in this crime.

RESPONSE. Just as Princes <note>original: *Principes*—referring to sovereign rulers and high-ranking magistrates</note> do not act wrongly when they move sharply against this crime, so they act badly—even most poorly—unless they do so with the greatest caution, prudence, and circumspection. It is so serious that it is not only forbidden to deal with this crime more freely or negligently simply because it is an "excepted crime" <term>crimine excepto: a legal category for especially heinous crimes, such as treason or witchcraft, where standard judicial protections and procedural rules were often suspended</term>, but one must watch over it with much more attention and care than in any other type of capital offense, lest an illegitimate and poorly judged trial be formed.

Therefore, even if I grant that in this excepted crime of Witches <note>original: *Sagarum*</note> it is permitted in some instances to proceed differently than the common manner used for non-excepted crimes, I nonetheless deny that it is permitted to act with *less* caution and circumspection than in that common manner. **REASON I.** This crime is most hidden, as all admit; it is usually carried out at night and among shadows and masks <note>original: *larvas*—can refer to masks, ghosts, or demonic apparitions</note>. Therefore, there is a need for great prudence and

# Doubt VIII. How cautiously Princes and those through whose deliberation they act must proceed, so that you may rightly bring these matters to light.

**REASON II.** We see that once a judicial process <note>original: *processum*</note> against witches <note>original: *sagas*</note> has begun, it is prolonged for several years and the number of those to be punished increases so much that entire villages are utterly consumed. Since this matter is so grave and so vast, can any amount of diligence be so great that it would not be fitting to apply it? Should we not fear that some error might intervene by which innocent people are entangled at the same time? Especially since, if even a single innocent person is entangled, it is necessary that countless others will be entangled immediately after, as I shall show further below.

### Doubt IX: Why they anxiously cast everything onto their officials.

...their <note>original: "suos"</note> [officials], because they are pressured by them. Another man retorted similar things to me some time ago when I was warning him; both had been appointed by that very Prince whom I mentioned at the beginning of this Doubt, who had shifted all responsibility from himself onto his subordinates.

Truly a most "pleasant" state of affairs! The Prince frees himself from the burden of care and the most diligent attention and casts it onto the conscience of the officials; the officials likewise free themselves and cast it back onto the conscience of the Prince—A onto B, and B onto A. The Prince says: "Let the officials see to it." The officials say: "Let the Prince see to it." 

What kind of circle is this? And which of them will answer to God? For when both these men and that one say "let the other see to it," no one actually sees to it. Truly, I can hardly express the grief in my heart when I am not permitted to point these things out, nor to advise that excellent and most pious Prince, for whom I would not hesitate to pour out my life.

**REASON VIII.** Such is the state of affairs at this time, that unless they occasionally [examine things] by themselves...

Lest the reader think I am exaggerating or repeating these points out of malice, let him hear the words of a certain great Prince’s Inquisitor—indeed, two of them. Recently, after they had read through the learned and prudent commentary of the most highly praised theologian of the Society of Jesus, Adam Tanner <note>Adam Tanner (1572–1632) was a prominent Jesuit theologian whose work "Theologia Scholastica" urged caution and legal rigor in witchcraft trials, making him a target for hardline witch-hunters.</note>, they dared to say that if they had caught the man himself, they would not have hesitated to cast him upon the **rack** <note>original: "equuleum" — an instrument of torture, often called the "wooden horse," used to stretch the body.</note>. 

Specifically, because he most prudently and solidly warns that the business of **witches** <note>original: "Sagarum"</note> must be handled with caution, and that judges will easily go astray if too much weight is given to their own discretion, and other similar points; to these most foolish men, this provided sufficient evidence <note>original: "indicium" — a legal term for a piece of evidence or a sign of guilt that justified the use of torture.</note> that even such a great theologian could be seized for torture. 

I do not believe that the most serene blood of the German Princes would not boil if they had heard, even with half an ear, such words from their own officials. Now let a Prince judge, if any reads this, or let the Councilors of Princes judge: with what moderation and skill have these men "armed justice" against lowly souls, poor women, and simple folk, when they have dared to strike out in this way against such a great man—not to say against his entire Order <note>The Society of Jesus (Jesuits).</note>? 

And yet, Germany endures such Inquisitors or secular and lay Commissioners, and Princes commit this entire matter to their consciences; these are the "most learned" men...

<term>legal consultants</term> <note>original: "jurium confulti"</note>. The result is that, indeed, a man would be looking out for his own safety very poorly if he were to set pen or tongue to this subject even in the slightest degree. I grieve for the sake of the **Princes**, who thus possess a quiet conscience even when it is in the greatest danger, since even their own **Confessors** have been deprived of either the freedom or the will to warn them. Three times lately I have taken up my pen, and three times again I have pulled back, lest I should try to instruct anyone by letter; for what does it concern me?

### Doubt IX. *Whether Princes [can have] a sufficiently free conscience if...*

Alas, however, that so many others remain silent, though it concerns them deeply, and they are the only ones who would be heard fruitfully if they were able to speak. In this **cautionary writing** <note>original: "monitorio scripto" — a text intended to warn or advise those in power.</note>, if you consider its essence, I do nothing other than advise **caution** <note>original: "cautela"</note>; I criticize the errors of certain people; and I show that certain proofs or signs used widely by some are of little importance. My goal is that **many innocent victims may be helped** <note>original: "innocentibus multis subveniatur"</note>. 

My approach is to be no more sharp than the situation demands and as befits a man of religion. I do not criticize anyone but the wicked, and then only in general; I do not touch upon the good, nor do I speak of them. There is, therefore, nothing harmful here that could displease good men and lovers of **equity** <note>original: "aequitas" — the principle of fairness that supplements or overrides strict statutory law.</note>. On the contrary, those who love equity and are guided by reason and **prudence** <note>original: "prudentia"</note> will rejoice that, day by day, a broader path is being opened through which one may advance toward the **citadel of truth** <note>original: "veritatis arcem" — a metaphor for the ultimate, secure discovery of the facts in a trial.</note>. 

Nevertheless, I do not doubt that if this work were to fall into the hands of the common crowd, there would be many **Judges of capital crimes** <note>original: "rerum capitalium Præfecti" — officials presiding over trials involving the death penalty.</note> who would be indignant and would shout it down <note>original: "exploderent" — literally to hiss or clap an actor off the stage; to reject with contempt.</note>. By that very reaction, however, they would identify themselves clearly enough for who they are and how much they truly love equity. But whatever the case may be, it remains a fact that there will be no one who dares to **warn the Princes** <note>original: "monere Principes"</note>, unless they themselves...

### REASON IX.

Unless Princes in these cases also occasionally cast a closer eye and gain some **first-hand knowledge** <term>experimentalem notitiam — knowledge gained through direct observation or personal experience rather than abstract theory.</term>; they will sin gravely if, when their officials later return to them with certain difficulties, they dare to decide what should be done. 

I will prove that they will sin: first, because they will necessarily decide poorly. I prove this because they will not understand the reports or the information given to them. And I prove this because the **ways of speaking used by the judges** <note>original: "novi juvenci sunt à Judicibus loquendi modi" — literally "the ways of speaking used by judges are like young steers," implying they are wild, unbroken, or unfamiliar concepts to those outside the court.</note> are new; they are not found in the linguistic treasuries or **dictionaries** <note>original: "Calepinis" — referring to the famous polyglot dictionary compiled by Ambrogio Calepino, which was the standard reference for scholars in the 16th and 17th centuries.</note> we currently use, but must be learned from that unique first-hand knowledge I mentioned.

Lest I be thought to be making this up, let the Princes test themselves: is there even one among them—after so many **pyres** <note>original: "busta" — literally funeral pyres or tombs, referring here to the mass executions of accused witches.</note> have been lit—who to this day knows what these phrases of the Inquisitors mean when they say, for example:

1. **Gaia's defense was heard, but it was not satisfactory.** <note>original: "Audita est Gaiæ defensio, non satisfecit." Gaia was a traditional placeholder name in Roman law, used like the modern "Jane Doe."</note>
2. **We have grave evidence against her.** <note>original: "Habemus gravia contra eam judicia." In this context, 'judicia' refers to legal indications or incriminating signs rather than final verdicts.</note>
3. **We proceed according to what is alleged and proved.** <note>original: "Procedimus secundum allegata & probata." A common legal maxim often used to justify strict adherence to procedural records over objective truth.</note>
4. **Titia confessed her guilt without torture.** <note>original: "Titia se ream fassa est sine tortura." Like Gaia, Titia is a placeholder name for an accused woman.</note>

Hence, if an **Inquisitor** <term>Inquisitor — an official appointed to investigate and prosecute heresy or witchcraft.</term> should report to the Prince what he commands to be done, for example, regarding **Titius the Priest** <note>original: "Titio Sacerdote" — Titius is a common legal placeholder name, like "John Doe."</note>, whether he should not be burned alive—a man who is not only overwhelmed by great evidence but even convicted to his face, and who nevertheless refuses to be converted or to repent? What, I ask, should the Prince reply here?

### Doubt X. Whether it is believable that God would permit [the innocent to be punished].

For first of all, this [Binsfeld’s] opinion opens a window to laziness for the Judges, so that they are not as exquisitely careful and diligent as they ought to be. Secondly, it eases the consciences of Princes, so that they do not care deeply about what sort of men—how good or how skilled in handling affairs—they appoint as Judges. Finally, it is also devoid of truth. The reasons are as follows:

**R E A S O N  I.** For why, I ask, would God not permit now, in this time, what He permitted in the past? In those days, not only many, but almost innumerable martyrs of Christ were subjected to unspeakable tortures and were even held guilty of this very crime of magic <term>magia</term> that we are discussing. Where was that axiom <note>An "axiom" is a self-evident truth or established principle; here, the author refers to the claim that God always protects the innocent from legal error.</note> hiding then—the claim that God would not permit so fierce a storm to rage against the innocent? Where then were the promises of divine law that Binsfeld cited just before? Where were the examples he brought forward, and that "greatest testimony," as he called it, of Cyprian? Were those martyrs not all innocent? Did they not truly worship God? Did they not call upon His name? Did they not have all their hope and trust placed in Him?

G.</term> <note>An abbreviation for the Latin *verbi gratia*, meaning "for the sake of example."</note>, He permits the sacred hosts <note>The consecrated bread used in the Eucharist, which in Catholic theology is the literal body of Christ.</note> to be trampled upon and handled in other foul ways; He permitted His only-begotten Son to be crucified alongside thieves, and other similar things. ### Question XII. Should investigations against witches therefore cease?
<note>original Latin: "Dub. XII. An igitur cessandum sit ab inquisitione contra sagas."</note>

*YOU MAY ARGUE I: Purging the Commonwealth <term>rempublicam</term> of such an atrocious crime of witches is so great and desirable a good that this seems a sufficient and just cause why one should not worry if a few innocent people perish.*

*RESPONSE: If they were to perish through no fault of yours and only indirectly, perhaps one or two would not be a concern; but as it stands, you perform an evil act by directly creating danger for them. Hence, these enormous evils are not a just cause to stir up danger for the innocent.*

*YOU MAY ARGUE II: Therefore, one must also abstain from wars, in which quite often not a few innocent people suffer the same destruction as the guilty.*

The reasoning is not the same: for it is one thing to act indirectly

Dub. XIII. What if such a danger threatens the innocent?

# Question XV. Who are those who most greatly instigate the Magistrate?

**THE FIRST** kind consist of those Theologians and Prelates <note>High-ranking church officials</note> who, content with their own speculations and private studies <note>original: "musaeolis," literally "little shrines of the Muses," referring to their secluded libraries</note>, enjoy the deepest peace. To visit the jails, to speak with the wretched, to stoop to the complaints of the poor—they consider such things to be beneath their dignity and a distraction from their scholarly duties. What, therefore, can they truly understand of these matters? And consequently, what advice can they offer to Princes that is worth hearing?

To these I add certain holy and religious men who are, however, plainly inexperienced in worldly affairs and the wickedness of men. Because they are simple and holy themselves, they assume that all Judges and inquisitors are equally upright in their own cases. They consider it a great sin if we do not venerate all public legal judgments as sacrosanct and incapable of error.

...[safety] will be achieved if the following Precautions <note>original: *Cautelæ*</note> are applied.

**PRECAUTION I.** Let Princes <note>In the Holy Roman Empire, these were the local territorial rulers who oversaw legal jurisdictions.</note> ensure above all else that those employed to direct or judge the cases of witches are thoroughly suited for a task of such great weight. I am not accusing anyone here, yet concerning the ignorance <note>original: *imperitia*, referring to a lack of legal or logical skill</note> of many, I could affirm that I frequently marvel at how poorly they discern the consequences of things—how they often believe the greatest weight lies in the flimsiest arguments against the accused, and conversely, how they consider of little consequence those things that hold weight and importance in favor of the accused. ### Question XVIII. Some Corollaries
<meta>Catchword from previous page: indiciis</meta>

...even if someone has been sentenced to torture based on evidence <note>original: *indiciis*; refers to circumstantial evidence or "indications" that suggest guilt but do not fully prove it</note>, they nonetheless ought not to be subjected to torture if there are contrary indications of innocence which prove innocence just as much as the former prove guilt. For one <term>presumption</term> <note>A legal assumption that a fact is true until it is disproven</note> rightly cancels out another, as you may see in the works of Menochius <note>Giacomo Menochio (1532–1607), a prominent Italian jurist known for his work on legal presumptions</note> on presumptions, Book 1, questions 29 and 30, and Mascardus <note>Giuseppe Mascardi, another influential legal authority on the law of evidence</note> on proofs, Book 3, conclusion 1224, number 4 and following. 

And when two contrary presumptions meet—namely, one of crime and one of innocence—the presumption that excludes the crime is always to be preferred, says Farinacius <note>Prospero Farinacci (1544–1618), a leading Roman jurist whose works on criminal law were standard across Europe</note> in question 38, number 112. Farinacius states that this is the common opinion of the learned Doctors, many of whom he cites, even if the evidence brought forward for the defendant were slightly weaker than that brought against him. 

But who, I ask, observes these things today? Who pays attention to see whether they are observed? I truly wonder at the conscience of those who do not better advise the consciences of Princes <note>The "Prince" refers to the sovereign ruler or governing authority of the territory</note>; but they remain silent.

No mention is made—not even the slightest—of the things she brought forward to clear the evidence against her, as if all those points had been rejected by silence alone.

Consequently, it became necessary, due to the complaints of the people, to send out others who were more skilled and discerning.

### Doubt 19. Whether concerning those captured under the name of Witchcraft presently <note>original: *Dub. XIX. An de capt. nom. Venef. mox*; "Doubt" refers to a "Dubium," a standard format for legal or theological inquiry.</note>

DOUBT XX.

# What should be thought concerning Torture or judicial interrogations? Whether they create a frequent and moral danger for the innocent?

I respond. Such is the general state of torture that when I turn over in my memory everything of this kind that I have seen, read, and heard, I cannot conclude anything else except that it creates a frequent and moral danger for the innocent. It fills our Germany with "witches" and unheard-of crimes—and not just Germany, but any nation that begins to try this same path. The reasons are as follows:

**REASON I.** The <term>tortures</term> <note>original: *tormenta* or *quæstiones*; the formal judicial process of using pain to extract a confession.</note> commonly used are by nature massive, and cause pains that are bitter beyond measure. It is the nature of extreme pain that, so long as one might escape it, one does not fear running even into death itself. Therefore, the danger is that many women <note>The Latin *multæ* is feminine, reflecting that the vast majority of those accused of witchcraft were women.</note>, to free themselves from the agonies of the **rack** <term>equuleus</term> <note>The *equuleus* or "little horse" was a wooden frame used to stretch the body, a common instrument of torture during this period.</note>, will confess to a crime they did not commit. They will lie about any sort of wickedness regarding themselves—whatever the <term>inquisitors</term> <note>original: *quæsitores*; the officials tasked with "seeking out" the truth through interrogation.</note> suggest, or whatever the accused themselves have previously imagined saying just to make the torture stop.

# DOUBT XX. What should be thought concerning Torture or interrogation?

...to me, certain men who had hung in **tortures** <note>original: *tormentis*; refers specifically to being suspended during interrogation.</note> because of the gravest crimes solemnly affirmed that no crime could be devised so great that they would not have most promptly taken it upon themselves, if by confessing to it they had been allowed to be released from such great agony for even a little while. Indeed, they said that rather than suffer themselves to be brought back to that same state, they would sooner leap headlong into ten deaths.

But if others are found who prefer to be torn apart rather than break their silence on the **rack** <term>equuleus</term> <note>The *equuleus* or "little horse" was a wooden frame used to stretch the body, a common instrument of torture.</note> (*as* Aelian *mentions regarding the Egyptians in his* Miscellaneous History, *Book 7, Chapter 8*), these are truly rare today and are often protected against all sensation of pain by **evil arts** <note>original: *non bonis artibus*; a common 17th-century euphemism for sorcery or magical charms used to numb the body against pain.</note>. 

Whence, not undeservedly, the law (*Law 1 of the Digest, On <term>Interrogations</term>*) <note>original: *de quaestionibus*; in Roman law, this specifically refers to the legal procedure of questioning under torture.</note> calls Torture a "fragile and dangerous thing." For it speaks thus:

*It is declared in the constitutions that credit should not always, nor yet never, be given to **interrogation** [by torture]: for it is a fragile and dangerous thing, and one which deceives the truth. For many, through their endurance or the hardness of the tortures, so despise the torments that the truth can in no way be squeezed out of them. Others are of such impatience that they would rather lie about anything than suffer the torments. Thus it happens that they confess in various ways, and [accuse] not only themselves, but also others...*

## REASON III.

### Whether by the duration and frequency of torture the innocent are induced to confess.

It is clear that there is no one—neither among the penitents who might accuse themselves, nor among the confessors who might ask—who raises a complaint; even though an obligation of **restitution and satisfaction** <term>restitutionis & satisfactionis</term> <note>In 17th-century law and theology, "restitution" and "satisfaction" meant the legal and moral requirement to compensate a victim for injuries or wrongful losses.</note> is attached to this matter. Therefore, it is certain to me that many have died from these most excessive tortures, many have also been rendered useless for the rest of their lives, and many others were so mangled and torn that when they were to be punished by beheading, the **executioner** <term>lictor</term> did not dare to bare their shoulders according to custom, lest he provoke the people to riot by such a cruel spectacle. Some even had to be "dispatched" <note>A euphemism for being killed or executed quickly.</note> while still on the way to the place of punishment, lest they fall down dead before they even arrived, and so on. Yet, there is still no one [among the judges or executioners] who does not maintain a most peaceful conscience, or who considers himself bound in the slightest degree in his conscience to make satisfaction for these injuries.

Now, to speak of the duration: indeed, the pain of torture is truly very rare if it burns for even half a quarter <note>original: "dimidium quadrantem." A quarter of an hour is fifteen minutes; half a quarter is seven and a half minutes.</note>—or rather, just this half-quarter alone; but what will it be if it lasts for a full quarter? What if for two quarters? What if for an hour? ### THIRTEENTH REASON 

The danger is further increased by the fact that in this already mentioned "industry of suggestion," not only have the examiners <term>quæsitores</term> <note>Interrogating judges or examiners responsible for the questioning.</note> become skilled, but even the lictors <term>lictores</term> <note>The assistants or executioners who physically handled the accused and prepared them for the rack.</note> themselves have made remarkable progress in it. This "art" succeeds with all the more success the less it is known to the Inquisitors—if, indeed, it is always unknown to them.

For when certain lictors prepare simpler accused women for torture <term>tormenta</term>, they first instruct them on which accomplices they should boldly name. They tell them that so-and-so has already been denounced three or four times by others, and warn them not to hesitate or refuse to denounce those whose guilt is already "well-established" and who will not escape regardless. They tell the women to follow their advice and that they will be merciful to them. 

This is what they do; but these wicked scoundrels also suggest what other women have confessed about the accused themselves, so that they might learn what they ought to confess about their own actions if they are broken by torture. From this, it follows that when they later confess the same things about themselves—using the same circumstances that others previously confessed about them—the examiners triumph marvelously and record it with great detail in the official records <term>protocollis</term>.

# QUESTION 21.

## Whether a woman accused of witchcraft can be tortured repeatedly.

The question must be distinguished so that these two points are understood to be asked:

I. *Whether she can be tortured again, who was once tortured and confessed, but afterward retracts her confession.*

II. *Whether she can be tortured again, who was once tortured but did not confess. I shall speak of both. Therefore:*

I RESPOND, first: *If any woman, having been once tortured, has confessed to the crime herself, but afterward retracts, [the authorities] maintain that she can be returned to torture even if no new evidence* <note>original: "indicia" — legal signs or clues that suggest guilt but do not yet constitute full proof.</note> *has come to light. And the 16th law of the Digest regarding questioning* <note>original: "lex 16 ff. de quæst." — referring to the section on 'De Quaestionibus' (On Torture/Inquiry) in the Corpus Juris Civilis, the foundation of Roman Law.</note> *must be understood to speak of this repetition when it says: the Divine Brothers* <note>original: "Divi Fratres" — the Emperors Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus, whose legal decrees were cited as precedent.</note> *ruled that questioning could be repeated.* 

The reasoning is: first, because a prior confession made during torments stands in place of "semi-full proof" <note>original: "semiplenæ probationis" — a legal status where the evidence is halfway to a conviction, requiring only a little more to finalize it.</note> and creates sufficient evidence, as Wesenbecius <note>Matthaeus Wesenbeck (1531–1586), a famous jurist whose commentaries were standard legal textbooks.</note> holds in this passage. Secondly, the prior evidence is not invalidated by such a retraction; and finally, if the torture could not be repeated, Lessius <note>Leonardus Lessius (1554–1623), a highly influential Jesuit theologian and writer on justice and law.</note> says this whole remedy would be without

...unless new and most urgent <term>indications</term> <note>original: "indicia" — in early modern law, these were pieces of circumstantial evidence (like a witness report or a "devil's mark") that provided the legal grounds to authorize torture.</note> are brought forward again. Thus *Claro, Menochio, Gregory of Toulouse, Farinacci, Dinus, Alberticus, Villabodus, Sylvester, Azor, Lessius* <note>The author is listing a "who's who" of 16th and 17th-century legal and theological authorities to show that his cautious approach is actually the standard "common opinion" of the experts.</note> and other Jurists and Theologians commonly agree. Note the words *more evident arguments*, so we may understand that greater evidence is required than that which sufficed for the first interrogation. Whence <term>Delrio</term> <note>Martin Delrio, a Jesuit and famous demonologist; the author uses Delrio's own authority to argue for restraint.</note> rightly says in Book 5, Section 9: *Torture is never to be repeated,* he says, *unless new indications of a different kind and more evident than the previous ones emerge, and unless the defendant is so strong and robust that they endured the previous torture in both mind and body.* So says he, entirely in accordance with the spirit of the law.

And the reason is manifest: for the previous indications brought against the accused woman, however grave they were, have been sufficiently driven out, weakened, and destroyed by the first torture; so that, as a result, the accused woman ought to be acquitted as one who has been legitimately cleared and <term>purged</term> <note>original: "purgata" — a legal term meaning the suspect has "washed away" the legal suspicion by surviving the torture without confessing.</note> of the crime. Indeed, the truer and more common opinion is that even "full proofs" are purged by sufficient torture, as *Prospero Farinacci* <note>An influential Roman jurist (1544–1618) whose work on criminal practice was used throughout Europe.</note> teaches at length against certain others in his *Criminal Practice*, book 1, title 5, question 40.

<header>...that he might be tortured more often.</header>

<term>Delrio</term> <note>original: "Delrius" — Martin Delrio (1551–1608), a Jesuit scholar whose work on magic and law was a standard reference in witch trials.</note> follows this in Book 5, Section 11, as do <term>Tanner</term> <note>original: "Tannerus" — Adam Tanner (1572–1632), a Jesuit theologian known for his cautious approach to the legal handling of witchcraft.</note> and others. Thus, a case cannot be returned to torture unless either other new <term>indications</term> <note>original: "indicia" — circumstantial evidence or signs of guilt that provide the legal basis for a judge to authorize torture.</note> are brought forward, by which the person is summoned once more into a new suspicion of crime, or it must be argued that torture can be inflicted on anyone without cause—which is unheard of and contrary to all equity.

Moreover, that the law intends for these new indications for a second torture to be more evident than the prior ones used for the first torture is established entirely according to reason. For when an accused person has accurately escaped the arguments by which they were first attacked, and is then attacked by others anew, it is a matter of natural instinct that we generally expect the new arguments to be more valid than the previous ones were. 

Furthermore, since a second torture is necessarily much more bitter than the first was—for in the first, the spirit was still upright and the strength brought to it was as yet unbroken—right reason certainly demands that one should not proceed to a torture so much more severe except for causes that are equally more severe. Therefore, let that which the law says be done: that is, the defendant may be returned to <term>questioning</term> <note>original: "quaestionem" — a technical term in Roman and Canon law referring to interrogation under torture.</note>; but with the condition that they are overwhelmed by more evident arguments—that is, hemmed in by new indications that are even more valid than the prior ones.

Indeed, we must add what <term>Farinacci</term> <note>Prospero Farinacci (1544–1618), a famous Italian jurist whose works on criminal law were cited across Europe.</note> teaches in Book 5, Question 38, number 77, following <term>Paris de Puteo, Angela, Marsilio, Aymon, Blanchus, Carrerius, and Guido...</term> <note>The author continues to list prestigious legal authorities to bolster the argument that his call for restraint is not personal opinion, but established legal precedent.</note>

# Doubt XXI. Whether [a woman] accused of witchcraft...
<meta>catchword: knows</meta>

...according to <term>Suzzaria</term> <note>original: "Suzzaria" — Guido de Suzzaria (c. 1225–1292), an influential Italian jurist.</note>, <term>Bossius</term> <note>original: "Bossium" — Egidio Bossi (1488–1546), a prominent legal authority from Milan known for his work on criminal law.</note>, <term>Clarus</term> <note>original: "Clarum" — Giulio Claro (1525–1575), an Italian jurist whose "Sentences" were a primary source for criminal procedure.</note>, <term>Menochius</term> <note>original: "Menochium" — Giacomo Menochio (1532–1607), a famous legal scholar specializing in "presumptions" or circumstantial evidence.</note>, <term>Francesco Personali</term>, <term>Bertazzuoli</term> <note>original: "Bertazzum" — Bartolomeo Bertazzuoli (1520–1588), a noted legal practitioner.</note>, and others: these <term>indications</term> <note>original: "indicia" — legal signs of guilt or circumstantial evidence.</note> must not only be stronger than the previous ones, but also of a different kind—that is, they must differ from the others in their specific nature and substance. 

For example, he says: the first indications concerned the bad reputation of the person under investigation, or their enmity with the person killed, and because of those, the defendant was tortured and confessed nothing. Later, a witness comes forward who testifies to having seen the same defendant wound the victim, or saw him with a drawn sword. Such are called **new indications**, because they differ from the first in their nature or substance. 

However, if the defendant previously had against him an indication of reputation proved by certain witnesses, and having been tortured because of them he persisted in his denial, he cannot be returned to torture again, even if additional witnesses come forward proving that same reputation. For such witnesses do not bring a *new indication*, but rather a *new proof* of an old indication. 

*So says he: and although these things are such that they are consistent not only with the laws but also with the most upright reason, and for that reason should be upheld in all crimes—even <term>Excepted Crimes</term> <note>original: "criminibus Exceptis" — particularly heinous crimes like witchcraft or treason where standard legal rights were often restricted.</note>—nevertheless, because the consciences of many are lax and harsh, being little concerned for the future life and judgment of another, it is customary in <term>practice</term> <note>original: "Praxi" — the actual application of law in the courts as opposed to theory.</note> for it to be observed far differently, as [one] acknowledges...*

<summary>This page defines the legal requirements for "new indications" of guilt needed to justify a second round of torture, emphasizing that the evidence must be of a different category (e.g., eyewitness testimony) rather than just more of the same (e.g., more people hearing rumors). The author notes that while this is the law, many judges in practice ignore these protections due to their harsh nature.</summary>

# D O U B T XXII,

## Why many Judges in these times are reluctant to acquit the accused, even if they have cleared themselves through torture.

I ANSWER. *I have not yet often seen—though in many places I could have very frequently seen—a woman dismissed who, by denying the crime during the first torture, had cleared herself. They are acquitted with the greatest difficulty and scarcely ever in truth, once they have been received into prison; and this might appear to be a Zeal for justice and a certain kind of fire of virtue. FIRST, *By hook or by crook* <note>original: "Per fas & nefas" — a Latin idiom meaning by any means necessary, whether right or wrong.</note> *they wish to have those whom they may burn, as I have already said in the preceding doubt; there is some sort of blind impulse, whether the fault lies with the judges or with the magistrates.*

<header>Doubt XXIII.</header>

## Under what pretext it may seem possible to allow the repetition of torture without new evidence.

**I ANSWER.** There is more than one pretext that judges of a looser conscience can use, and which is now commonly and vigorously employed everywhere.

**PRETEXT I.** Bartolus, the legal consultant, in his commentary on the law *unius* in the Digest regarding interrogations <note>original: "ff. de quæstion." refers to the *Digestum* or *Pandectae* of Justinian's civil law, specifically the section on judicial questioning under torture.</note>, wishes it to be placed within the judge's discretion whether someone who confessed nothing in the first interrogation can be returned to the Rack <term>Equuleum</term> <note>The *Equuleum* (literally "little horse") was a rack-like torture device used to stretch the limbs.</note>. Baldus holds the same view in his commentary on Law 2, number 10, at the end, of the Code regarding things done through fear <note>original: "C. quod metus causa" refers to the *Codex Justinianeus*.</note>. Likewise, Paris de Puteo, Marsilius, Cataldus, Menochius, and others cited by Claro and Farinacci in question 38, number 87. This is truly right and excellent for the mindset of the judges: for they will say they are following the opinion of **Bartolus** and **Baldus** and the others cited, and wherever it pleases them, they will judge that it is necessary to repeat the torture. 

If you should say that the judge's discretion ought nonetheless to be regulated according to the laws, as the **Doctors** <note>In this context, "Doctors" refers to the *Doctores Iuris*, the high-ranking legal scholars and professors whose commentaries shaped European law.</note> rightly observe, they will respond that in the case of "exceptional crimes" <note>original: "exceptis criminibus" — a legal category for heinous crimes like treason or witchcraft where standard legal protections for the defendant were often suspended.</note> it is permissible to overstep the laws. Thus, their discretion will always be completely free, and no one, no matter how much they have erred, can ever be summoned or punished.

### Doubt XXIII. By what pretext it may seem possible to obtain [the repetition of torture]

...that it can then be done when the first torture was not sufficient. So says Giulio Claro <note>original: "Clarus," referring to Giulio Claro (1525–1575), a prominent Italian jurist.</note> in Book 5, Question 64. What, however, should be judged as "sufficient," depends on the discretion of the Judge, says Martin Delrio <note>original: "Delrius," referring to Martin Delrio (1551–1608), a Jesuit theologian and author of a famous treatise on magic and witchcraft.</note> in Book 5, Section 9; Joos de Damhouder <note>original: "Damhouderus," referring to a Belgian jurist (1507–1581) known for his manuals on criminal law.</note> in *Criminal Practice*, Chapter 38; and others everywhere. And in this case, judges are accustomed (these are the words of Giulio Claro in the place cited): **when they order the accused to be taken down from the first torture, they have it written that they order him to be taken down with the intent of repeating it <term>animus repetendi</term>, etc.**

Very correctly, this will also fight for the benefit of those lax judges: for they will say, whenever they wish, that the previous torture was not sufficient. Indeed, they will call every torture "insufficient" which has not yet extorted a voice from the accused. This will be a common starting point for building a false accusation <term>calumniæ</term>. Therefore, let the accused be tortured: if he confesses, it is well; if he does not confess, the torture was "insufficient," let it be repeated tomorrow; if even then he does not speak, the torture was still "insufficient"—let us proceed.

By which pretext <note>original: "Quo præt[extu]." For torture that is broken up and spread out over time afflicts a person incredibly more than torture that is continuous. Certainly, such a notable excess of pain cannot be decreed without a most serious sin, for the reason given above in Doubt 21.

## PRETEXT V.

The authority of Jacob Sprenger and Heinrich Institor <note>Heinrich Kramer (c. 1430–1505), known by his Latinized name Institoris.</note>, the authors of the *Hammer of Witches* <note>original: "Mallei maleficarum," the most famous medieval treatise on the prosecution of witches, first published in 1486.</note>, will greatly support the preceding pretext. These men were once sent to Germany by the Apostolic See as inquisitors of heretical depravity. For they expressly teach that a person who does not confess can be tortured multiple times, not by way of repetition, but by way of **continuation**. Their words in Part 3, Question 14, page 513, are as follows:

> But if the accused cannot be led to terror or even to the truth [by the threat of torture], then he must be questioned <note>In legal Latin, *quaestionandum* refers specifically to judicial interrogation under torture.</note> on the second or third day for the purpose of **continuing** the torments, not **repeating** them (because they ought not to be repeated unless new evidence <term>indicia</term> <note>Legal "indications" or circumstantial evidence that suggest guilt.</note> has come to light), and then the sentence shall be delivered before him in the manner that follows: "And we..."

<summary>The author argues that pausing torture only to resume it the next day is a form of psychological and physical cruelty that exceeds legal limits. He cites the Malleus Maleficarum to show how inquisitors used the semantic loophole of "continuation" versus "repetition" to bypass laws forbidding multiple torture sessions.</summary>

"The aforementioned Judge, we assign to you, such a person, such a day to continue the questioning so that the truth may be heard from your own mouth." <note>This is a template for a judicial decree, where "such a person" and "such a day" act as placeholders for specific names and dates.</note> Thus they speak, all too brilliantly. "We will not repeat the torture," they will say; "far be it from us to do so without new and most significant evidence. We will only continue it on another day until the truth shines forth. We know it cannot be repeated; that is against law and reason. We do not wish to be so inhumane and cruel; we will only continue it. We have learned that **continuation** is possible, and we follow authors skilled in this matter—men who have served as Inquisitors <note>Ecclesiastical officials charged with detecting and suppressing heresy.</note> throughout Germany, theologians, and members of religious orders." Thus they will defend themselves. I do not know what to say—that religious men and priests could speak in such a way and play games in such a bitter matter.

To me, this seems like irreligious cruelty. Truly, from the beginning—indeed, I have often feared it before now—I suspect that the aforementioned Inquisitors first imported this entire multitude of witches into Germany by their "indiscreet" <note>original: "indiscretis." In this context, it means both "lacking judgment" and "undivided."</note> tortures; or rather, I should say most truly, by their "discrete" and divided tortures. <note>The author is making a biting pun. The law says torture cannot be repeated (indiscreet/continuous). By "dividing" it into separate days (making it "discrete"), the judges claim they aren't repeating it, while actually making the suffering worse.</note>

### Question XXIV.

How can a meticulous <note>original: "scrupul[osus]," meaning a judge who is overly precise or strict in applying the letter of the law to justify harshness.</note> judge allow three rounds of torture, to the point that if someone were accused of five different crimes and suspected based on circumstantial evidence, and three tortures and examinations were already exhausted on only three of those offenses, he should then be tortured for the remaining crimes as many times as necessary until the examination regarding them is completed and finished? This is argued just as a defendant who has been "sufficiently" tortured—that is, two or three times—and has confessed the crime against himself, can then be tortured a fourth or fifth time to reveal his accomplices. They claim this is permitted because he was never specifically tortured regarding the matter of his accomplices.

This is how Tanner <note>Adam Tanner (1572–1632), a Jesuit theologian who eventually became a critic of the scale of the witch trials.</note> says Delrio <note>Martin Delrio (1551–1608), a Jesuit whose writings were frequently used to justify the legal procedures of the witch hunts.</note> teaches in Book 5, Appendix 2, Question 34. I do not have that specific appendix by Delrio at hand to verify it; but if it is so, what, I ask you, will happen in the crime of **Witchcraft** <note>original: "Magiae."</note> where so many different crimes are usually interconnected? How wide a path will be opened for Judges to multiply the sessions of torture? May God forbid the monstrosity that would result from this. Finally, it is clear from what has been said that, under the appearance of Justice, the Inquisitors <term>Inquisitor: An official, usually a theologian or lawyer, authorized to uncover and punish heresy or witchcraft.</term> possess such power to repeat torments that there is no kind of person—provided they can be subjected to torture—who would not appear to be thoroughly infected by the plague of magic.

If this is the case, then the judges who decreed such things were most unjust. If this is so, then the tortures were also most unjust, and therefore invalid and void under any law. Consequently, they cannot be used to Titia's disadvantage, nor can any argument be drawn from them against her. Therefore, Titia cannot be judged as a witch <note>original: *saga*</note> because of them, nor can she be tortured anew. And even if she were tortured, she still cannot be burned alive—neither as "obstinate" if she remains silent, nor as "confessed" if she admits guilt—since both the obstinacy and the confession are legally void.

<header>Doubt XXV. *Whether there is new evidence for torture.*</header>

To the Personal [representatives] and others. O great Emperor, how many people in this Germany of yours are perishing daily in this way, and have already perished? Yet you bear no blame, for you wait for the complaints of those petitioning you so that you can help everyone.

**REASON III.** I frame the same argument in another way: the judges say that Titia <note>A traditional legal placeholder name, similar to "Jane Doe"</note> still appears to be a witch <note>original: *saga*</note>, and she can be returned to torture because they have now found "new evidence" <note>original: *indicium*</note>. But what is this evidence? They claim she used a spell <note>original: *maleficio*</note> to overcome the previous tortures. But how do they prove this very thing? They say it is because the tortures were so severe that they could not be overcome otherwise. 

I accept this premise and conclude: therefore, the judges who inflicted such tortures were most unjust, as it was not naturally possible to resist them except by a spell. Therefore, ultimately, the judges possess "new evidence" only because they were most unjust; if they had not been most unjust, they would not have it. 

Titia’s "new guilt," therefore, rests entirely upon the injustice of the judges. Remove this injustice, and they have nothing new against Titia. Indeed, even if you keep the injustice, they still have nothing, since whatever is built upon unjust and invalid torture is itself invalid and null. Thus it is now clear how ignorantly and self-contradictorily these thoughtless men speak.

### REASON IV.
Even if we grant that Titia <note>A standard legal placeholder name, similar to "Jane Doe."</note> could not have resisted those tortures except by the help of either a demon or of God, why do they now assert that it was done by the help of a demon rather than by the help of God? For indeed, when Titia is so brutally tortured, she was either truly innocent of the crime with which she was charged, or she was truly guilty. If the former is true, what is more credible than that **GOD** helped someone so innocent when they were being so cruelly tormented? If the latter is true, then even if we grant that a demon rather than **GOD** helped her, the judges still should not presuppose that this happened or that Titia was truly guilty, since that very point is still the question at hand. Indeed, it is precisely because they are ignorant of her guilt that they are searching for "new evidence" <note>original: *indicium*</note> in the first place.

### REASON V.
If the fact that Titia confessed nothing during the most severe tortures is, in their eyes, new evidence of a crime, then these most severe tortures were clearly inflicted on her in vain and for no purpose. For what was the goal? Was it to find out for certain whether Titia was guilty or not? But they could have just as easily written down that she was guilty before they started (if that is what they wanted). For in that case, the argument they intended to make afterward, they could have made a little earlier: namely, that Titia will either confess her guilt under those tortures, or she will not. They say that some defendants go mute and fall asleep <note>original: obdormiscere; witch-hunters often claimed that the Devil cast a "spell of sleep" on witches so they would not feel pain or confess during torture.</note>. However, I do not wonder at this as much as I wonder that the most learned writers have based almost the entire weight of their doctrine—which they have proposed to the world regarding the affairs of witches <note>original: "Sagarum"; a common term for witches in legal and theological Latin</note>, and which the world seems to have embraced—upon this single, fallacious foundation. Let us see, therefore, by what arguments they are moved, and let us respond to them.

### ARGUMENT I. It is a grave sin to lie against oneself in a case involving death, or at least against one’s neighbor; therefore, it is not believable that the accused would do so.

*Response.* This argument of theirs has always seemed weak to me. For in the first place, the best theologians deny that it is a mortal sin if someone, to avoid grievous torments, charges themselves with a false crime for which they must be punished by death. The reason is that a person is the master of their own reputation, and they do not lie harmfully since they are not bound to preserve their life through such torments—which are themselves more grievous than death. Hence, they are not bound to revoke the confession later, since by not retracting it, they do no injury to anyone. See Lessius <note>Leonardus Lessius (1554–1623), an influential Flemish Jesuit theologian known for his works on justice and law</note>, and those he cites in Book 2 of *On Justice and Law*, Chapter 11, Doubt 7, number 41.

Then it is also probable what Pedro de Navarra <note>A 16th-century Spanish jurist and canon lawyer</note> holds in Book 2, Chapter 3, number 251, and Sylvester <note>Sylvester Prieras (1456–1523), a Dominican theologian who wrote the *Summa Sylvestrina*, a standard reference for confessors</note> in the *Summa*—

<summary>Spee challenges the "learned writers" who believe tortured confessions are true, arguing against the theological claim that a prisoner would not lie about their guilt because lying is a mortal sin.</summary>

For this may be presumed if they do not wish the consciences of the accused to be cared for except by the unskilled and those unmindful of their duty." Therefore, here follow the instructions, omitting others already well known, which will be most useful to record.

# Question 30: What instructions should be given?

I hear now from all sides that members of religious orders <note>original: "religiosos," referring to members of orders such as the Jesuits, Franciscans, or Dominicans rather than secular parish priests.</note> are being employed in these cases. Their superiors should take care to send those who are endowed with the spirit of Christ our Lord: men who are mild, gentle, and praised for their devotion. They should be of accurate judgment and proven prudence in the Lord—men who have gained experience in reaching human minds, understanding them thoroughly, searching the secrets of hearts, and also in bringing sinners to contrition. They should not be impetuous or slaves to their own emotions, but should weigh everything against the standard <note>original: "libellam," literally a level or plumb-line used by builders to ensure a wall is straight.</note> of reason and sound doctrine. The superior should also take care, through companions assigned to them, to find out if these priests are being judged as acting imprudently or otherwise; for they often allow many things that are very much in need of correction.

### DOCUMENT XVI.

It may be asked, what should a **Confessor** <term>Confessor</term> <note>A priest who hears the private confessions of the accused and offers spiritual guidance and absolution.</note> do if (which is not impossible, as you may see in **Tanner** <note>Adam Tanner (1572–1632) was a prominent Jesuit theologian. Like the author of this text, he was critical of the legal methods used in the witch trials of the Holy Roman Empire.</note>) he should learn of someone's innocence through a confession or from some other source? Should he reveal it? If he does reveal it, a danger might arise of violating the **sacramental seal** <term>sacramental seal</term> <note>The "Seal of Confession," the absolute duty of a priest not to disclose any information learned during the sacrament of confession, even under threat of death or law.</note>—specifically, if he were hearing the confessions of others as well and remained silent about them. For by his silence regarding the others, he would imply that they were not like the first [innocent] one.

But if this danger is absent—for instance, because he is not hearing the others, etc.—and if he also believes his efforts before the **Judge** will not be in vain, nor cause new tortures for the accused, nor lead to some other trouble such as a great scandal among the people, then I do not see why he not only *can* but *should* try to provide aid. For so **charity** <note>original: "charitas," referring to the Christian duty of love and care for one's neighbor.</note> commands, and so does the Scripture: *Rescue those,* it says, *who are being led...* <note>original: "Erue eos, inquit, qui ducuntur," quoting Proverbs 24:11: "Rescue those being led away to death; hold back those staggering toward slaughter."</note>

<header>Question XXXII. For what reasons [one might proceed to...]</header>

# QUESTION XXXII.
## For what reasons is it lawful to proceed to torture?

**I answer.** Above all, the greatest care must be taken that, since torture is so dangerous and bitter, it is not resorted to except for grave reasons—that is, preceded by very urgent "indications" <term>indicia</term> <note>original: "indicia"; in 17th-century law, these were circumstantial pieces of evidence or signs of guilt that fell short of "full proof."</note> that would, as it were, overwhelm the accused. Legal experts <term>Iurisperitis</term> use the term "indications" for all those things from which it can be inferred that, for example, Titius <note>original: "Titium V. G."; Titius was a standard placeholder name in Latin legal texts, similar to "John Doe."</note> has committed a crime. I shall categorize these into three kinds: Great, Greater, and Greatest; and let us see which are required for Arrest, which for Torture, and which for Condemnation.

I. FOR ARREST <term>capturam</term>, "great" indications are required. The reason is this: to cast anyone into a significant hardship, such as imprisonment <term>captivitas</term>, based on trivial reasons, is at odds with both justice and charity. From this it follows that just as imprisonment is made more severe—whether by the social standing of the person to be arrested or for other reasons—so too is there a need for stronger evidence.

II. FOR CONDEMNATION <term>condemnationem</term>, the "greatest" or most urgent indications are required, clearer than the midday sun, which constitute full proof; that is,

III. **FOR TORTURE** "great" indications are not sufficient, since torture is in many ways more severe than mere imprisonment. However, the "greatest" indications—or full proofs—are not required. Instead, those we called "greater" indications are sufficient and required: those so firm and clear, and almost certain, that any prudent person could rightly place great trust in them, as all authorities commonly teach. Today these are called "semi-full proofs" <term>probationes semiplenae</term>, though you might better call them "almost full." That is, they prove to such an extent that, while they do not plainly convict, they come very close to full proof—much like the moon when it strives toward its full light, passing beyond its half-crescent stage. ### QUESTION XXXIII.

->Whose duty it is to decide which specific indications are such that they can be held as almost full proofs.<-

I ANSWER, Since a single general rule cannot be given regarding this matter as to which specific indications <term>indicia</term> <note>In this legal system, "indications" are specific facts or clues—like being seen at a crime scene—that suggest guilt but do not yet equal "full proof."</note> open the way to torture—that is, which constitute "half-full" proofs <note>original: "semiplena probationes" — a legal term for evidence that is more than a suspicion but less than a conviction.</note>—there are those who wish it to belong to the discretion of each individual judge. So says Brunnus <note>Conrad Brunn (1491–1563) was a German jurist and author of a major treatise on legal evidence and torture.</note> in his treatise on indications and torture, part 2, question 3. ->Question 34: Whether reputation alone<-

# QUESTION 34.

## Does reputation alone, unsupported by other clear and firm proofs, provide a sufficient indication for torture?

I answer 1. **It does not.** This is the opinion of *Julius Clarus* <note>A leading 16th-century Italian jurist whose works were standard textbooks for criminal law across Europe.</note> in his *Sentences*, book 5, question 21, number 1, along with the entire consensus of the Doctors <note>Refers to the "Doctors of Law," the highest recognized academic and legal authorities of the time.</note>, quite a few of whom he cites, but whom we—according to our custom—omit here. The reasons are as follows:

**REASON I.** It is an axiom among Jurists and Theologians that reputation <note>original: 'fama' — referring to public rumor, common talk, or a person's general standing in the community.</note> in criminal cases does not constitute proof, but functions only in the manner of an accuser. Therefore, just as a person cannot be tortured based on a mere accusation unless the accuser provides some proof, so too it is in this case, etc.

**REASON II.** Reputation provides the judge with a different method for discovering the truth—namely, through an <term>inquisition</term> <note>original: 'inquisitio' — a formal judicial inquiry or investigation conducted by the court itself to see if there is substance to a rumor.</note>—says *Lessius* <note>Leonardus Lessius, an influential Jesuit theologian known for his writings on justice and law.</note> in his work *On Justice and Law*, chapter 29, doubt 17, number 156.

**REASON III.** Reputation is an <term>indication</term> <note>original: 'indicium' — a legal sign, clue, or piece of evidence that suggests guilt and can legally justify more severe measures like torture.</note> that is very remote from the crime itself, and likewise very deceptive, as we experience daily. This is stated by *Clarus* in the place cited above, and by *Farinacius* <note>Prospero Farinacci, a prominent Roman jurist whose works on criminal procedure were cited throughout the Holy Roman Empire.</note> in question 47, along with those they cite. Moreover—to use the words of Farinacius—the indications for torture must not only be plausible, but grave and urgent...

<summary>The author argues that common rumor or public reputation ("fama") is an insufficient legal basis for applying torture. He supports this by citing major legal authorities who maintain that rumor is too deceptive and remote from the facts to serve as anything more than a prompt for further investigation.</summary>
