## Question XXXIV. *Whether reputation alone*

[...we have] fallen, where everything everywhere is full of slanders and insults. Whenever anything sinister happens to us, those men and women who might have enchanted us are immediately fixed in our minds; people run to <term>diviners</term> <note>original: 'divinatores' — fortune-tellers or folk-healers often consulted by the superstitious to identify the "source" of a misfortune.</note>, most honorable persons are burdened with suspicions, and the poison of rash judgment is spread in secret—all the more harmful and wicked because it is done more secretly and safely while the **Magistrate** sleeps. Hissing whispers creep through homes and the city; people join one another, until gradually, having gained strength, they burst out into an open but illegitimate reputation. 

Not even then does the **Magistrate** wake up to investigate who first spread this most pestilent air; instead, at the sound of this illegitimate voice, he girds himself for action: he searches, he arrests, he tortures, and he wishes those whom that unfair rumor has oppressed to be found guilty by right or wrong. 

A shameful thing! First, the poisonous tongues ought to have been investigated; they should be cut out from these detractors and slanderers and fixed to the **pillar of infamy** <note>original: 'infamem columnam' — the pillory or a public post where criminals were shamed.</note>. If even a few of this kind—I do not say a hundred (as would indeed be fair?), but even five or six—had been publicly hanged, then finally, from the outcry of a reputation thus corrected at least slightly, some small weight for suspicion could be found.

For the inference should have been made thus: Unless reputation is legally proven, the sign is invalid; therefore, even if we must proceed, we must not do so based on an unproven reputation.

# Whether the Magistrate is bound at this time, of his own accord and without being pressed by anyone, to take action against detractors and slanderers?

I respond: Magistrates or Princes are bound at this time—if indeed they ever were—to restrain with the harshest established penalties those "poisonous tongues" that cast accusations of the crime of magic <note>original: "magiae crimen" — specifically referring to witchcraft or sorcery, which was often sparked by neighborhood gossip.</note> upon their neighbors and stir up suspicions, even if no one is currently pressuring the officials to act. In doing so, they must ensure for their subjects that public reputation <note>original: "fama" — in early modern law, a person's "fama" was a protected legal asset, similar to property.</note> is kept as pure and free from the license of slander as the very air we all breathe. The reasons are as follows:

**R E A S O N I.** Everywhere, detraction and slander are growing far too strong, and Christian charity <note>original: "Christiana charitas" — the fundamental theological principle of love and kindness toward one's neighbor.</note> is being offended to the highest possible degree. I have even heard men say that, because of this situation—where a person's reputation is not protected and legal trials proceed based on mere rumor—they would rather live among the Turks <note>The author refers to the Ottoman Empire; this was a common rhetorical device used to suggest that even a non-Christian "enemy" state might offer more legal stability than a Christian land caught in a "witch-hunt" panic.</note> for a time, provided they were allowed to remain faithful to their religion. This certainly seemed quite inappropriate to me, and I rebuked them for indirectly insulting the Magistrates...

### Doubt XXXV. Whether the magistrate is bound of his own accord to act.

For even if someone should win their case in court, a **slander** <note>original: "calumnia"</note> aired publicly at a **tribunal** <note>A seat of judgment or a court of law.</note> is spread so much more widely than one wrapped in silence. From this, it happens that if anything subsequently occurs—no matter what—that could be interpreted in a negative light, anyone might soon twist it in that direction. Thus, even if a person is acquitted by the court's judgment, people nevertheless silently judge for themselves that the accusation was not brought forward entirely for no reason. Something always sticks; a slander, once heard, cannot be so easily erased from the memory of the common people. Instead, at the slightest occasion, a reckless **suspicion** <note>original: "suspicio"</note> may break out. 

Wicked men might also count these individuals among the **defamed** <note>original: "diffamatos"; people whose public reputation has been legally or socially compromised</note>, whose names some **Inquisitors** <note>Official investigators, often associated here with the witch trials.</note> use when seeking out people to investigate. The common people still remember that these individuals were once "defamed" by slander, but they more easily forget that they were acquitted, or they attribute the acquittal to the favor and corruption of the judges. 

Examples of this kind are daily occurrences. Indeed, those who are captured and **tortured** <note>original: "torquentur"</note> in the meantime more easily accuse these same people—since they are already "defamed"—when they are forced to name accomplices. And so, these are most wretched times: for either you remain silent in the face of the slander forced upon you, and by this very fact [you seem] to be guilty...

<header>Doubt XXXVI. Whether public report alone is sufficient.</header>

"There could even be a crime," *he says*, "of such difficult proof that **public report** <note>original: "fama"; the general reputation or rumor regarding a person's character or actions in their community, which held legal weight in early modern law.</note> alone would suffice, as I have sometimes seen observed in practice." Thus he speaks; and **Farinacius** <note>Prospero Farinacci (1544–1613), an influential Roman jurist whose works on criminal law were widely cited across Europe.</note> follows Clarus in *Question 47, number 11*, as does **Menochius** <note>Giacomo Menochio (1532–1607), a famous Italian jurist known for his expertise on legal presumptions.</note> in *On Presumptions, Book 1, Question 89, number 34*. **Binsfeld** <note>Peter Binsfeld (c. 1540–1598), a German theologian and auxiliary bishop of Trier, known for his influential treatise on the confessions of witches.</note> also, in his *On the Confessions of Evildoers, page 288*, says that a Judge ought to be more prompt and ready to proceed to torture in cases of **atrocious** <note>original: "enormibus"; crimes so severe they were considered "outside the norm," often triggering harsher legal procedures.</note> and hidden crimes, because those things done in secret are more difficult to prove. For this reason, he adds that the following legal maxim arises: in **clandestine and hidden matters** <note>original: "clandestinis & occultis"</note>, proofs by way of **conjecture** <note>original: "conjecturas"; logical inferences drawn from circumstantial evidence rather than direct eye-witness testimony.</note> suffice due to the difficulty of the matter, whereas in other cases they would not be sufficient. Finally, concluding on the **crime of witches** <note>original: "crimine sagarum"</note>, he says: "Who can doubt that the crime of **sorcerers** <note>original: "maleficorum"; those who practice harmful magic or "maleficium."</note>, which for these and other reasons is most hidden, can be investigated through **torture** <note>original: "tortura"</note> based on lighter evidence?"

These are the reasons:

**REASON I.** Law 1 of the *Digest regarding torture* <note>original: "lex 1. ff. de quæstionibus"; a foundational reference to Roman civil law (the Digest) which dictated that torture was a tool of last resort to finalize an almost-proven case.</note> states that one should only resort to torments when the defendant has been brought so close to proof (meaning **full proof**) that only a confession seems to be lacking. Moreover, the law speaks universally, making no distinction between types of crimes; and where the law does not distinguish, we should not distinguish unless another factor compels us. But if the arguments and evidence by which the defendant is pursued do not constitute at least nearly full proof, the defendant cannot properly be said to be "brought close" to full proof, since this term implies a state of nearness. It is just as one does not say the moon is already "approaching fullness" when it is still a thin crescent; it is only said to be so when it has proceeded at least beyond the half-moon stage.

<header>Proving that which does not suffice in common crimes.</header>

If a matter is hidden and shrouded in darkness, then there is a need for a greater light, not a lesser one, to illuminate it. If it is of difficult proof, then there is a need for greater arguments, not lesser ones, so that it may be proven either fully or almost fully. Therefore, if you reject **conjectures** <note>original: "conjecturas"; in legal terms, these are inferences drawn from signs or circumstances that do not reach the level of certain proof.</note> in a common crime where proof is not difficult, you must certainly reject them much more so in a crime where proof is difficult.

**RESPONSE:** *It is true that he who lacks greater things may be content with lesser ones; however, he would err if he attributed the same force to both, and wished to use the latter for the same effect as the former. ## REASON VI.
The opposing opinion overturns <term>Logic</term> <note>original: "Dialecticam"; referring to the formal rules of reasoning and evidence used in both philosophy and law.</note>. I demonstrate this with the following example: they say that the testimony of an <term>infamous witness</term> <note>original: "testis infamis"; a person whose legal standing or character was compromised, such as a criminal or social outcast.</note>, an accomplice, or a partner in crime does not suffice for torture, nor does it constitute nearly full proof. If, however, the crime is an "excepted crime" or is otherwise difficult to prove, they claim it then suffices and validly proves the case for torture.

I say that this plainly opposes Logic. This is proven because testimonies of this kind, according to all Logic, are arguments called "from authority." Regarding such arguments, the unshakable doctrine of Logic is this: that their value and weight depend on the authority of the person testifying—that is, on their truthfulness in speaking. Thus, just as a person is prudently presumed to be more or less truthful, the argument likewise carries greater or lesser force of proof and value.

# Question XXXIX: Whether she can be condemned.

*The prince will have to be informed. But I omit examples. Indeed, I believe this to be unjust. These are the reasons:*

### REASON I. No one can be condemned
of a crime that is not established with certainty. Regarding this woman I mentioned, it was not established with certainty; therefore, she could not be condemned. The premise must be proven: For if it were established, it would be either because she herself confessed or because she had been legally convicted; neither of these was true here, therefore it was not established. It is clear she did not confess. I also prove she was not convicted as follows: If she had been convicted, she would not have been tortured; but she was tortured, therefore she was not convicted. This is clear from what was said above (And see Farinaccius <note>Prospero Farinacci (1544–1618) was a famous Italian jurist. His work *Praxis et Theorica Criminalis* was the standard legal textbook of the era.</note>, *question 38, number 4*). Torture is applied as a **supplement to proof** <note>original: "supplementum probationis"; in Roman-canonical law, if evidence was strong but not "full," torture was used to extract a confession to complete the case.</note>. She was tortured three or four times; therefore, the proofs required supplementing three or four times. If they required supplementing, however, they were certainly not **full** <term>plenae</term> <note>Full proof (*probatio plena*) was the high legal standard required for a death sentence, usually requiring two eyewitnesses or a confession.</note>. If they were not full, they did not convict the defendant; therefore, she was not legally convicted, therefore her crime was not established with certainty, and therefore she could not be condemned.

Thus, the argument should not be framed as: "They are sorcerers; therefore, their retraction must not be heard." Rather, it should be framed thus: "They retract at the very moment they know they are about to stand before the tribunal of eternity." It is a rare thing, even then, for a person not to be mindful of their soul's salvation; therefore, one may prudently doubt whether they are actually sorcerers at all.*

Therefore, whatever retraction occurs before death does not happen because of the persistence of those advising the defendant on their salvation.

...at the **bench of justice** <term>bench of justice: the formal courtroom setting where a prisoner’s sentence was officially read and their confession was publicly "ratified"</term> they ratify the lie; and they do not retract it until the very moment they are falling into the embrace of death, finally safe from further torture. But they are soon led back to the torture chamber, where they learn that no torture is more bitter than the one which follows the "free" speaking of the truth.

For some inquisitors are not satisfied even when, upon hearing the mention of being sent back to torture, the accused suddenly renounces that freedom, ratifies their previous confession, and expresses regret for the retraction, wishing it undone. No, they still order them to be taken back and tortured anyway, so that they might finally announce "most freely" at the bench of justice—for they use this phrase, and let the reader now learn what it truly means—I say, announce "most freely" that they are guilty. 

This is done with great exaggeration before the common people about how great the malice of these evildoers is, who, even though they are eventually found to be openly guilty, had previously mocked the court in such a way. As a result, anyone in the future would have to be utterly insane to dare speak at the bench in any way other than what pleases the judges. <header>Question XL. Whether the revocation of a crime [has weight]</header>

**Response.** I grant that they are ignorant, but I completely deny that they are excused. They could have known all these and similar things, if only they had wanted to; why did they not know? I will show most clearly that they were able to know.

Everyone—both the **Magistrates** and their **Officials**—proclaim that the crime of magic <note>original: "magiae"</note> is most hidden and spreads most secretly. Yet this very "most hidden" crime is not so hidden from the Magistrates that they do not think themselves capable of dragging countless defendants of this crime into the light every day. They know and recount entire **"Iliads"** <note>a literary reference to Homer's *Iliad*, here meaning a vast or epic quantity</note> of villainies and plots which the witches <term>witches: "sagae" in the original, referring to those accused of sorcery</term> supposedly carried out in their most secret meetings. 

If, therefore, they are able to know these and similar things which they claim are so deeply submerged in darkness, how can they not know things that are done openly in the light of day? Therefore, they will not stand innocent before God, nor even before men, since it is difficult to stretch a **cloak of such affected ignorance** <note>meaning ignorance that is intentional or faked to avoid responsibility</note> over their actions. 

And let these things be said in passing as the occasion arises, though they ought to be considered; and from this, it is also somewhat less surprising why there is such a great number of witches in **Germany**. Let the remaining judges take note and imitate the notable **strategy** of that Inquisitor already mentioned, by which they ensure that henceforth no defendants give them trouble with a **revocation** <note>original: "revocatio"; the act of a prisoner withdrawing a confession they previously made under torture</note>. Thus, our entire dispute—whether any weight should be given to revocations—will collapse.

## DOUBT XLI.

### What is to be presumed concerning those women who are found dead in the prisons.

I ANSWER: *If any woman accused of witchcraft <term>witchcraft: "maleficium," literally "evil-doing," specifically referring to harmful magic in a legal context</term> who has not yet legally confessed under torture <note>original: "in tormentis"</note>, nor been convicted, is found dead in prison; it ought to be presumed that she died a natural and honorable death, unless the contrary is sufficiently discovered from certain signs. This stands against the practice of many unskilled men who, as soon as they understand that a soul has expired in prison, immediately judge that she was strangled by a demon and order her to be dragged out beneath the gallows <note>original: "patibulum"</note>, as I myself have seen more than once. <header>Those who died in prisons.</header>

...Many until now throughout Germany have laid down their lives in prisons, yet not a single one of them, they claim, died from torture or the miseries of the cell. For who has ever heard of such a thing? No: "the demon led them all out from here; he broke the necks of them all." And by what proof? Who was present? Who saw it? "The executioner says so" <note>original: "carnifex," the official responsible for torture and executions, whose testimony was often the only evidence in these cases</note>. He, of course, is the one who does not want it heard that he tortured the prisoner beyond measure. He is a man of ill-repute and usually a scoundrel; yet because he alone handles and lays out the corpse, he is the only one who can be a witness. Does our entire faith in the matter rest with this one man? Even if you ask many questions, every final and ultimate proof eventually goes no further than his own judgment. 

In this matter, one must rightly wonder why it is that while in all other affairs almost no one possesses such authority that they do not leave some room for doubt, in this most serious of businesses, the authority of the executioner alone is enough to erase all doubt. Whatever he pronounces is held as the absolute truth, as if Jupiter himself had spoken <note>A classical reference to the king of the gods, meaning the executioner's word is treated as divine, unquestionable law</note>. 

Thus he spoke. Because these words pleased me greatly and I wished to pursue this line of reasoning further, I turned to the Governor: "I pray," I said, "that we do not remain ignorant of the facts which we are discussing here for our own amusement. Let witnesses be sent from this very table to the scene of the matter, so they may report the certain truth back to us. And since the official <term>lictor: a guard or officer of the court responsible for handling prisoners</term> is at hand, so that the corpse might be inspected even now, let them go with him and examine it diligently. In this way, whatever [comes] of it..."

# Question 41: What should be presumed regarding them, etc.

...that they cannot be deprived of **church burial** <note>original: *Ecclesiasticâ sepulturâ*; burial in consecrated ground according to the rites of the Church</note>; and yet, they are deprived.

II. IV. This same **infamy** <note>original: *infamia*; a legal and social status of disgrace that resulted in the loss of certain rights</note> is passed down to the family and their descendants. This must be considered even more grievous when the family lineage is more honorable. If each of these points is significant on its own, and if **restitution** <note>original: *restitutio*; the legal and moral obligation to repair a wrong or restore a reputation</note> is required both in the **court of conscience** <note>original: *conscientiæ foro*; the internal moral judgment of the soul before God</note> and in the public court, it is difficult to judge what snares those men are walking into—those who, relying on such flimsy reasons for belief, proceed as if they have no memory, completely unconcerned. Nor can they hide behind a veil of **ignorance**, for they were bound by their official duty to take the greatest care to ensure they were not ignorant.

<page-num>291</page-num>
<header>QUESTION XLII.</header>

# When can one judge with a safe **conscience** <note>original: *conscientia*; the internal moral sense of right and wrong, particularly in legal and theological decision-making</note> that a discovered **corpse** <note>original: *cadaver*</note> was strangled by itself or by a **demon**?

I respond: *This can be judged from these signs.*

1. If the neck is entangled in a rope.
2. If the head is twisted, and that plainly toward the back; for it is not sufficient if it is merely turned toward the shoulders to one side; which is a point to be noted.
3. If lines appear on the throat which were not there the day before; in which case, however, the judgment of a **physician** <note>original: *medici judicio*; an early insistence on the necessity of forensic medical expertise in legal matters</note> is required.
4. If—which could not happen without great external force being applied—the first vertebra of the neck is displaced from its position so that it protrudes backward; for only then can **strangulation** <note>original: *jugulatio*; literally "slaughter" or "cutting of the throat," but here used for a violent death of the neck</note> be presumed without rashness, and the corpse be dragged beneath the **gallows** <note>original: *furcam*; the frame used for hanging, where the bodies of those deemed "unclean" were often buried in disgrace</note>, unless again, as I said above, there is cause to suspect the **jailer** <note>original: *commentariensem*; the official responsible for the custody of prisoners and the prison register</note>. ### Question XLIII: On the marks of witches, whether they provide evidence for torture

...I saw it not, nor shall I believe it unless I have seen it. I see this daily: that the deceits of men are infinite, and the credulity of even great men is often shameful. Because these men are too high-ranking to meticulously <note>original: *ad unguem*; literally "to the fingernail," a Latin idiom meaning to examine something with extreme precision</note> examine such minutiae themselves, they embrace almost any fables, record them in their commentaries, and impose them upon the world. Meanwhile, because I neither believe nor deny, I will say what I feel until the matter is better examined and taught by the wise and learned. And so, to the proposed **doubt** <note>original: *dubium*; a technical term in scholastic writing for a disputed question or legal problem</note>:

**I ANSWER I.** It is sought in vain whether **marks** <note>original: *stigmata*; these were believed to be insensitive spots on the body where the Devil had "sealed" the witch</note> can be evidence for torture. The reason: Even if I were to grant that it is permitted to search for them through an **executioner** <note>original: *lictorem*; in this period, the executioner was a social outcast, often considered "infamous," yet he was the one tasked with searching the bodies of the accused</note> on the naked body of the accused woman, I would think it fitting that there must first be an excessively **half-full proof** <term>half-full proof (semiplena probatio): a legal standard in Roman-canonical law meaning circumstantial evidence strong enough to justify torture, but not strong enough for a final conviction</term>. Since it is not permitted to torture without such proof, it should also not be permitted to strip a woman thus before an **infamous scoundrel** <note>original: *infami scurrâ*; a derogatory reference to the executioner, emphasizing the sexual shame and loss of dignity for the accused woman</note>—which for that sex is sometimes more grievous than torture itself—unless that proof is already met. Once half-full proof against the accused has been obtained, what need is there for another sign from these marks to justify torture?

**I ANSWER II.** Before proceeding from marks, as if from full proof, to condemnation, these following things must be considered by the judges...

<header>Doubt XLIV. Whether [those accused of] magic should be denounced [by accomplices].</header>

### REASON II.
In the criminal constitution of **Charles V** <note>The *Constitutio Criminalis Carolina* of 1532, the first body of German criminal law, which standardized legal procedures across the Holy Roman Empire.</note>, which one must observe within the Empire, when the **indicators of sorcery** <term>maleficii; literally "evil-doing," but specifically referring to harmful magic or witchcraft in a legal context.</term> are recounted, the denunciation of two or more accomplices is not included. Surely this ought to have been included if the Emperor had thought that any weight toward [justifying] torture resided in such accusations.

### REASON III.
If the opinion of our adversaries were to be accepted, it would fall within the power and will of infamous and wicked persons to burden and blacken the good name, reputation, and person of honorable men. This is absurd and dangerous to the innocent, as you will gather sufficiently from what follows.

### REASON IV.
Either those women who at other times denounce others truly are **witches** <note>original: "sagæ"; a term specifically used for female sorcerers or witches in these legal texts.</note>, or they are not. If they are not, then how can they know anything about accomplices whom they do not have? They lie about themselves and about others so that they might free themselves from torture; therefore, these denunciations are of no weight if the accusers are innocent. If, however, they are guilty or truly witches, not even then do their denunciations have any weight: for by their very nature they must be assumed to be liars, having employed the **Demon as their Master**. Therefore, their truthfulness is non-existent, and thus there is no **proof**—

However, so that this may be better understood, I distinguish and say that there can be two types of **infamous persons** <term>infames; individuals who have lost their legal standing or "good name," which traditionally barred them from giving testimony in court.</term>: some who are infamous in their life or morals—that is, criminals. Regarding the first kind—the criminals—just as they are turned away by positive law, so too can they be admitted in **excepted crimes** <note>lat: "exceptis criminibus"; certain "hidden" crimes like witchcraft or heresy where standard rules of evidence were relaxed because they were so difficult to prove.</note> and those otherwise difficult to prove, since it is not contradictory for a criminal to be truthful.

Now, testimony is built upon authority, since it carries no weight except from the authority of the speaker; therefore, the testimony of such infamous persons wavers. If it wavers, then in a most grave matter where a person’s life is at stake, it is rightly rejected; right reason dictates this, and it is not merely positive law that prescribes it. For it is surely against the nature of the thing, and entirely against all reason, that you should establish a conclusion based on the authority of one whom you admit has a ruined reputation <note>original: "conclamatæ authoritatis"; literally "cried out against" or "hopeless" authority.</note>...

I. This lacks reason; or if it does not lack it, let that reason be provided, and I shall yield.

<header>Doubt XLVI. Whether at least accusations should be believed</header>

# DOUBT XLVI.

## Whether accusations <note>original: "Denunciationibus"; in this context, the naming of accomplices during a witch trial</note> should at least be believed, if it is infallibly certain that the accusers have truly converted and wish to speak the truth.

*I ANSWER. At last, it might seem so; but it should not seem so to me, nor to any prudent person who chooses to consider the matter more closely. These are the reasons.*

REASON I. Judges are accustomed, if any retract accusations they have previously made, to return those individuals to torture; and the executioners themselves are often the ones to threaten them with this. Driven by their own particular zeal for "uprooting the weeds" <note>A biblical reference to Matthew 13:24-30, often used by inquisitors to justify the execution of suspected heretics or witches</note>, they diligently warn the accused of this beforehand so they are not unaware of the consequences. Therefore, even if Titia <note>a common legal placeholder name, like "Jane Doe"</note>, a truly converted woman, had sincerely repented, she would still not dare to stop ratifying the accusations she had made previously. Consequently, if she continues to ratify them, it does not immediately prove that they were true; for even a truly penitent person can fear such grave punishments and, through the fear of them, continue a lie. Human fragility is great.

Those who have not tasted torture do not know how much those who have tasted it dread it beyond all measure. Because of this, it happens that few can be persuaded to consistently retract even their false accusations.

Let them therefore retract at least some of them, so that they may unburden their conscience as much as they can, while at the same time avoiding the repetition of torture—which they would not avoid unless they left at least one or two accusations unretracted. The reader will easily understand how much evil is created by leaving these few unretracted; for judges everywhere conclude from this very fact that the one or two names not retracted along with the others are therefore all the more certainly guilty. Consequently, they believe they must punish <note>original: "animadvertendum"; a legal term for judicial notice leading to punishment</note> that person even more severely if she continues to deny the charge.

The matter is truly dangerous from every side, and I do not wish to elaborate on it further, so long as this remains clear: Titia <note>a common legal placeholder name, like "Jane Doe"</note> can be a true penitent, and yet, if she had previously made any false accusation, she might leave it unretracted for fear of undergoing torture again.

### SECOND REASON

However much a witch <note>original: "saga"</note> who makes an accusation might be penitent, and even if this were infallibly certain and she truly wished to provide a truthful account, her accusations would nevertheless be deceptive because of the danger that the witches themselves are being deceived. For it is established and even admitted by our opponents that witches are not always physically <note>original: "realiter"</note> transported to their gatherings and dances <note>original: "tripudia"; referring to the ritual dances associated with the Witches' Sabbath</note>, but are often moved through imagination alone. This occurs when a demon—either by his own power or by using natural medicines <note>original: "medicamenta"; likely a reference to the "flying ointments" or hallucinogenic salves often mentioned in trial records</note>—stirs the imagination in various ways. As a result, they believe they have been present, seen things, and done things which were never actually seen or done anywhere, just as happens to those who, in sleep, are mocked not by real things but by the images of them.

There are many examples of this matter which are circulated everywhere and well known; for the sake of brevity, we omit them. ### THIRD REASON

Furthermore, even if we assume that a judge were certain that the accusers belonged to that class of people who are physically—not just through imagination—transported and gather together, he still cannot prudently rely on these denunciations. For a judge to act wisely, he must not only be certain that the witness (let us call her "Titia") <note>Titia and Gaia are standard placeholder names in Latin legal texts, similar to "Jane Doe" or "Jane Roe."</note> is not lying when she says she saw "Gaia" at the meeting, but he must also be sure that the following logic is sound: "Titia saw Gaia at the gathering; therefore, Gaia was truly present at the gathering." 

For how can the judge know whether the devil did not perhaps present a phantom image of Gaia there, so that she was thought to be present while she was actually very far away? Because this issue presents such difficulty, it must be dealt with more extensively in the following Doubt.

<header>Doubt XLVIII. What are the arguments of those who [strive to prove that the demon cannot represent the innocent]?</header>

I respond:

I. *This argument proves too much and therefore proves nothing: for it would prove that infinite other things which were truly done were not done, simply because these things were "unread and unheard of" by Delrio. They would surely be indignant and contend that God permits new things every day. Why, then, should they not grant me this: that among so many new things—hitherto unread and unheard of—which God permits to the demon in these assemblies <note>original: "conventibus," referring to the "Sabbath" or secret gatherings where witches were alleged to meet with the Devil</note>, these false representations also occur? I shall say that this is simply another one of those "new things."*

III. *Those who are denounced because they were supposedly seen in the assemblies are certainly held to be guilty, and are certainly believed to have been there in the body. Therefore, they are tortured for as long as it takes until they confess. And if some overcome the tortures and do not confess, they are nevertheless burned alive as "obstinate" <note>In legal terms of the time, an "obstinate" prisoner was one who refused to confess despite "proof," which was often taken as further evidence of the Devil's help</note>. ## Doubt XLVIII. *What the arguments are of those who*

*deny that there are any who, once arrested and forced by the violence of punishments to declare themselves guilty, have already meditated upon what narratives they wish to weave, so that they might appear to have lied convincingly—lest if anything should fail to match up, they be returned to the torture-shackles <note>original: "in nervum repetantur"; an idiom referring to being returned to prison or subjected to renewed torture</note>. I also know what resolutions I have given to many regarding these very cases of conscience: to what extent it is permissible or not to lie against oneself or others under torture without committing a mortal sin; so that indeed, in many places, many remarkably good people are terrified. Therefore, this argument of Binsfeld <note>Peter Binsfeld (c. 1540–1598), a German theologian and bishop who wrote influential works justifying the witch trials</note> does nothing but help me against him. For I conclude thus: if Binsfeld has acquired so little experience or knowledge in these matters that he is so ignorant of things that are widely known everywhere, what weight should finally be given to him and similar learned doctors in these cases? Let them sit in their study <note>original: "musaeo"; in this period, a scholar's private library</note> and continue what they have done most usefully until now: sending out theological treatises to us. But as for the cases of the accused, I beg that men of such great authority not touch them, unless they have at least eventually leaned their ears closer to the prisoners and approached them saturated with the filth <note>original: "padore"; the stench and squalor of 17th-century dungeons</note> of the prisons—which, as I know from experience, is accustomed to stir the spirits and mental images, so that we might philosophize much more mercifully than we otherwise would.*

### Doubt XLVIII. What are the arguments of those who [discuss] other matters common in those rites, such that the infernal actor <note>original: *infernalis histrio*; a metaphor for the Devil, suggesting he stages deceptive "plays" or illusions</note> seems to do nothing there so much as indulge in fashioning mere masks, specters, and false images. 

Since everyone admits this to be the case, any judge, whoever he may be, will surely doubt with prudence whether the demon’s license to fashion all kinds of specters might not also extend to the creation of other personas in these places—especially those existing in mortal sin. <note>Spee is arguing that if the Devil can create illusions of goats and monsters, he can certainly create an illusion of a specific human being to frame them.</note> He will also wisely fear whether the one said to have been seen in those places at that time was truly the person themselves, or rather some empty mask presented to the eyes. 

From this, however, it by no means follows that if someone is seen committing robbery, theft, or adultery in any other place that is not subject to such illusions or phantasms, I must then also suspect that I have been deluded by a specter. For the reasoning is far different. <note>Spee distinguishes between everyday crimes and the "supernatural" setting of a Sabbat; he argues that while we can trust our eyes in normal life, we cannot trust them in a place defined by demonic deception.</note>

It also shows how poorly he accused us of having "closed eyes"—for he claimed that we do not see the things which he believed he saw in the argument he put forward. One could respond in other ways as well, but what I have answered is sufficient.

# **Doubt XLVIII.** What are the arguments of those who claim that if the Devil were permitted to frame innocent people, too many great harms would result for the commonwealth <note>original: *rempublicam*; referring to the state or the well-ordered community</note>.

***Response 1.** Let us assume this is so. But how can you be certain that God does not permit things that result in great harms to the commonwealth? God allows the demon to transport witches <note>original: *sagas*</note>, to supply them with potions <note>original: *pharmaca*</note> for harmful magic <note>original: *maleficia*; magic intended to cause injury or death</note>, and other similar acts. None of my opponents disputes this. Do no harms arise from these? Therefore, unless it is proven by other means that God forbids the appearance of the innocent in those diabolical games <note>referring to the Sabbat or "witches' dance"</note>, it is useless to deny it.*

***Response II.** By denying the very premise. For what harm, I ask, will flow into the commonwealth from these illusions? Is it that the innocent will be considered guilty? That they will be tortured, and so on? I respond: I deny that they will be considered guilty or tortured by prudent and wise judges. I concede it might happen with foolish and mindless ones. Furthermore, my opponents' reasoning is flawed. They say that if the innocent are represented, the harm is that they will be judged guilty and tortured. They are presupposing that anyone seen in this way **must** be considered guilty. Yet this is the very heart of the question: should those represented in such a way be considered guilty? Thus, they are arguing in a circle: Why should those seen in the dance <note>original: *saltu*; the rhythmic dance of the Sabbat</note> be rightly held guilty? Because God [would not permit] innocents* <note>The sentence ends abruptly here as it reaches the bottom of the page; the catchword "centes" indicates the next page begins with "innocentes."</note>

<summary>The author argues against the idea that God prevents the Devil from framing innocent people, suggesting instead that the "harm" of innocent people being tortured is the fault of foolish judges who believe demonic illusions, rather than a failure of divine providence.</summary>

Furthermore, as for the claim by Binsfeld <note>Peter Binsfeld (c. 1545–1598) was a suffragan bishop of Trier and a major proponent of the witch trials; he argued that God would never allow an innocent person to be framed by the Devil.</note> that it is a privilege of the "children of God" that such a thing is not permitted, this was already refuted above in Doubt 10; look for the answer there.

# Doubt XLVIII. What are the arguments of those who, etc.

[reputations] : since I think the greatest part are innocent.

# What are the arguments of those who want trust to be placed in the accusations of witches, and who say they are sufficient for torturing those who have been named?

*Many arguments are brought forward, but because they easily collapse, we will set them out in order and resolve them.*

### ARGUMENT I.
A judge is bound to question a male or female sorcerer <note>original: *maleficum, seu maleficam*</note> about others, and the accused man or woman is bound to answer concerning others; Therefore, the guilty sorcerer is to be believed and their accusation <note>original: *denunciationi*; specifically, the naming of accomplices</note> must be upheld. This is proven as follows: For if trust were not to be placed in them, it would be in vain for the judge to be bound to ask, and for the accused to answer. Thus says **Binsfeld** <note>Peter Binsfeld (c. 1540–1598) was an influential German theologian and bishop who wrote a famous treatise supporting the reality and prosecution of witchcraft</note> on *page 248.*

*Response I: We who maintain that trust should not be granted to the accusations of witches, consequently deny that the judge is bound to attend to such accusations or to question the accused.*

*Response I (continued): Even if we concede that the judge is bound to question a guilty sorcerer about accomplices, it does not follow from there*

*nevertheless, it does not follow, as they [the proponents of the trials] wish, that we must immediately believe them if they say they saw accomplices at the gatherings <note>original: *conventibus*; referring to the "Sabbath" or witches' meetings</note>, or similar things which cannot be proven otherwise. For the judge is bound to ask for this reason: because it is possible that some other specific circumstances and added proofs might be provided in the testimony which would clearly implicate those being denounced—though I do not recall specific examples here and now, who can doubt that this could occasionally happen? Therefore, the judge will ask; I do not forbid that. But he will not believe the accuser unless proofs are added that clearly show the accuser is not lying. Furthermore, regarding what was allegedly seen at the gatherings, he will not believe it for the reasons I have mentioned above.*

### ARGUMENT II.
It is accepted by the judgment of all theologians, as well as canonists <note>experts in Church law</note> and civil lawyers, that a person who has confessed to their own crime should not be questioned regarding the secrets <note>original: *conscientia*; literally "conscience," but here referring to the private knowledge of the guilt of others</note> of others. If they were questioned, legal proceedings do not follow based on this testimony, nor is the person believed according to the law. Yet, despite this general rule, those crimes called "excepted crimes" <term>excepted crimes: *crimina excepta*; particularly heinous crimes like treason or witchcraft where standard legal safeguards for the defendant were often suspended</term> are exempted; in these cases, the accused must be questioned about others, and they must be believed. Therefore, their confession provides proof; otherwise, there would be no distinction between "excepted" and "non-excepted" crimes. Thus says **Binsfeld** <note>Peter Binsfeld (c. 1540–1598), a prominent suffragan bishop and witch-hunter</note> on *page 252.*

Response I: I deny that otherwise there would be no distinction between "excepted" and "non-excepted" crimes. For this is the distinction: in excepted crimes, it is not necessary to observe in every detail the common procedure prescribed by law for other cases. However, the rule that accomplices—who are liars by their very nature—should not be believed unless other circumstances and proofs convince us they are not lying, is not something prescribed only by law, but by nature itself, from whose law no exception is granted.

Response II: There are many more excepted crimes <term>excepted crimes: *crimina excepta*; heinous crimes where usual legal protections were ignored</term> than just witchcraft. Therefore, let what is said in the objection be true in those other excepted crimes; and there, if they so wish, let them believe the accusations <note>original: *denunciationibus*</note> of accomplices. In this crime of witchcraft alone, however, I do not agree that they should be believed, specifically because of those particular reasons I gave above, which are not found in the same way in other excepted cases.

### ARGUMENT III. One must stand by and adhere to the rule until an exception or a failure of the rule is demonstrated; but the laws on which we rely as our rules hold that the accusations of sorcerers <note>original: *maleficorum*</note> must be upheld; therefore [they must be believed].

The minor premise is proven from the final law of the Code *Concerning Sorcerers and Astrologers* <note>original: *Codex de maleficis & mathematicis*; a specific section of the Code of Justinian, the foundation of Roman law</note> which mandates that sorcerers be subjected to "due questioning" <term>due questioning: *debitae quaestioni*; a legal euphemism for judicial torture</term> in order to make their partners in crime known; and therefore, it judges that their accusations should be upheld.

# ### Doubt XLIX. What the arguments are of those who denounce [others].

To deviate from the letter of the law, from reason, and from common opinion is the height of rashness. Thus writes Binsfeld <note>Peter Binsfeld (c. 1540–1598) was a German bishop and theologian influential in the witch trials of Trier; he argued strongly for the validity of confessions and denunciations.</note> on page 253.

*Response I. It is true that the rule must be stood by and adhered to until an exception or a failure of the rule is demonstrated. It is also true that to deviate from the letter of the law and common opinion is rash, unless it is done with good reason. But we say that we are deviating from the rule, the letter of the law, and common opinion for good reason and by demonstrating a failure [of the rule]. We have already done this abundantly above.*

*Response II. There are two kinds of things that can be asked of sorcerers <note>original: *maleficis*; specifically those accused of performing harmful magic</note> concerning others.*

I. Concerning accomplices, if they had any, in the killing of humans or animals, in the inflicting of damages, and in similar crimes.

II. Concerning the locations of their assemblies <term>assemblies: *conventus*; the gatherings or "Sabbaths" where witches were alleged to meet</term>, their games, those who have mastered the "great art" <note>original: *artem magnā*; likely referring to advanced magic or secret occult knowledge</note>, and those seen there, etc.

I say, therefore, that the laws are to be understood as referring to questions of the first kind; and we concede—if our opponents so insist—that some credit may be given to them in questions of the first kind, especially if they also add circumstances that agree and from which signs arise regarding the truth of the accusation <note>original: *denunciationis*</note> that would satisfy a prudent and wise man. However, [credit] is not to be given in questions of the lat-

## Doubt 49. What the arguments are of those who denounce others, and why—even if they might be believed regarding accomplices in other crimes—they should not be believed in the crime of witchcraft when they speak of their assemblies; let these be considered again and we shall satisfy them abundantly.

## ARGUMENT IV. Witches are robbers, and more than robbers; they are conspirators with demons, they are guilty of high treason <term>high treason: *laesae Majestatis*; literally "injured majesty," the highest crime against a sovereign or God</term>, they are sacrilegious, they are traitors to their country, they are heretics, etc. But robbers, conspirators, those guilty of high treason, sacrilegious persons, traitors to their country, and heretics are believed when testifying against their accomplices; therefore, witches should also be believed. Binsfeld <note>Peter Binsfeld (c. 1540–1598), a German theologian and influential proponent of the witch trials.</note> says the same on page 254 and following.

### *Response. The logic applied to witches and to others is not equal: for there are particular reasons stated above why, even if others can be believed, witches nevertheless ought not to be believed. This is specifically due to their unique malice, their lying nature, and the particular presumption of falsehood in that crime on account of various illusions and uncertainties. Hence, it is not permitted to argue from other crimes to the case of witches, and Binsfeld is vehement here in vain.*

## ARGUMENT V. Those who speak the truth must be believed, otherwise human faith <note>original: *fides humana*; the basic trust required for society and the legal system to function</note> would perish; but it commonly happens that accomplices in this crime denounce...

# Doubt XLIX. What are the arguments of those who insist on accusations in a district against a person not yet accused or burned?

*II. Since such women <note>Referring to innocent women forced to name "accomplices" under torture.</note> do not know any others, they are mostly accustomed to naming those about whom there is already a common rumor, or those who have been imprisoned or burned before on that charge.*

*III. Now, where I am currently staying, not a few names recently denounced by various people are known to almost the entire city. These cases are therefore delayed for now while the rumor grows; after a year, however, the proceedings will begin based on this rumor. Oh the times! This is the "zeal" of Germany <note>original: *hic Germaniae est Zelus*; a sarcastic critique of the fanatical rush to execution in German territories.</note>.*

For from his own words, I form these <term>enthymemes <note>A logical syllogism where one of the premises is implied rather than stated.</note></term> as follows:*

*I. The demon is most unwilling for his followers to betray their true accomplices; however, he is not unwilling—indeed, he cannot be—but rather is most willing that they name and kill the innocent. Therefore, it must be thought that they would rather name the innocent to please their most willing master, than name the guilty against his most unwilling wish.*

*II. The demon forbids—indeed, as the same author said elsewhere, he compels them by oath in their gatherings <note>original: *conventibus*; the "Sabbaths" or meetings of witches</note>—not to name each other; however, he never forbids them from naming the innocent, nor does he guard against it with an oath. Why then would these most submissive female servants name those whom he forbids rather than those whom he does not forbid?*

*III. If they name true accomplices, the demon’s kingdom will be diminished. If they name others, it will not be diminished. Why therefore would they name the former rather than the lat—*

<summary>Friedrich Spee uses logical deductions (enthymemes) to dismantle the argument that the Devil's supposed "unwillingness" to let witches confess proves the truth of their accusations. He argues that the Devil would actually encourage the naming of innocent people to protect his own and spread more destruction.</summary>

**Response II. Concerning the *minor premise* of the syllogism.** <note>In logic, a syllogism is an argument where a conclusion is reached from two previous statements; the "minor premise" is the second of these statements.</note> For those who must name others are either true and real witches <note>original: *sagae*</note>, or they are not true, but "nominal" only—so to speak—meaning they are those who, coerced by the force of torture, took upon themselves a crime of which they were actually free. If they are true witches, I deny the minor premise. For they would name the innocent promptly, willingly, and readily, for the reasons given before; but if now, everywhere, those who must name others can only be driven to do so with great labor and the force of torture, I shall then argue instead that they are therefore not true witches, but nominal ones. For I shall completely turn the argument brought forward by my adversary back against him in this manner:

True witches, if they must name others, will be prompt to name at least the innocent, as the adversary concedes; but now, everywhere, those who name others are not prompt to name any at all <note>original: *etiam nullas*; implying they do not even name a single person without being forced</note>, as the same adversary will concede. Therefore, those who now everywhere name others are not true witches. It is a perfectly formal <term>syllogism<gloss>A logical structure where a conclusion follows necessarily from the premises.</gloss></term>.

## Doubt XLIX: What are the arguments of those who denounce others?

...of beggar boys <term>puerorum mendiculorum</term> <note>Children, especially those living on the streets, were frequently used as "witch-finders" or witnesses because they were easily manipulated.</note> who are either hired by ill-willed people, or—as it is easy to deceive those of that age—are so surrounded by a certain art of examination and deceptive little questions <term>interrogatiunculis</term> that they are trapped. And so, when a goat was recently lost—which I mention here for the sake of the ridiculous—it turned out a soldier had simply led it away. Yet, that same goat was said to have been consumed in a gathering of witches <term>sagarum</term> by various people who were already being punished (or were about to be punished). There are many such examples which I omit because I am hurrying toward the conclusion. Perhaps at another time we shall collect them. Let the Magistrate <term>Magistratus</term> know that he is being mocked by his Officials <term>Officialibus</term> in a way that is both amazing and lamentable.

->Doubt L.<-

## Whether a judge can safely embrace either opinion: either ours, which disregards these denunciations, or that of others, which values them highly.

I respond: *He cannot safely embrace the opinion of the opponents. These are the reasons.*

**REASON I.** The safer path is to be chosen in cases of doubt. <note>original: *Tutior via in dubiis eligenda est*</note> Although this rule serves as a piece of advice in other matters, it carries the force of a divine command when there is a danger that injury might otherwise be done to one's neighbor, as the Casuists <term>Casistæ</term> <note>Scholars of moral theology who studied specific "cases of conscience" to determine the right course of action.</note> teach and as I also stated above in *Doubt 8, near the end.*

**REASON II.** I have shown through sound examples that the opinion of the opponents does not stand on solid ground. Therefore, either the judge must establish their position better by bringing forward other arguments and refuting ours, or he will be bound to follow us.

**REASON III.** The laws <term>Jura</term> require that in doubtful cases, favor should be shown to the defendant rather than the accuser <note>original: *in dubiis reo potius quam actori faveatur*</note>, *according to Rule 11 of the Law in the Sixth Book.* <note>Referencing the *Liber Sextus Decretalium*, a major collection of canon law.</note>

**REASON IV.** A judge ought to follow the safer interpretation, *according to the chapters "Ad audientiam" and "Significasti" 2, concerning Homicide.* <note>These are specific legal precedents in canon law that emphasize caution when a person's life is at stake.</note>

**YOU WILL SAY I.** *But Binsfeld <note>Peter Binsfeld (c. 1540–1598), a suffragan bishop of Trier and a staunch proponent of the witch trials. He argued that the state must be aggressively "purged" of witchcraft.</note> cries out that in this way, the commonwealth will never be purged [of witches].*

The argument brought forward for the other opinion—namely, that trials are advanced in this way, etc.—does not prove it is more useful for the commonwealth <term>republica</term>, but on the contrary, that it is harmful. For trials to be advanced and such grave executions to be facilitated based on the lightest indications <term>indiciis</term>—that is, based on the most fallacious testimonies resting on the "truthfulness" of lying witches <term>sagarum</term>—is as harmful to the commonwealth as those grave evils which can follow from these cases when they are handled rashly, as I said above in Doubt 8, Reason 3.

### YOU WILL SAY III.
A judge harms the good whenever he spares the wicked. Those who permit many to be killed so that they might spare one are cruel, etc. So says the same man from Rinteln <note>Johann Georg Gödelmann (1559–1611), a legal scholar at the University of Rinteln who, while moderate for his time, still allowed for the use of denunciations in witch trials.</note> on page 153. But—

**I respond:** This is true in principle, but it is not relevant to the matter at hand. For first of all, he who wishes to identify the wicked only through the most fallacious denunciations of the wicked will instead spare the wicked and cut down the good; thus, he will harm the good in two ways. Secondly, those who do not care if they also destroy several good people at the same time in order to kill one wicked person are the ones who are truly cruel. Finally, it is not just one person who is spared when the denounced are spared; for many are spared, and they are spared deservedly, since it has not yet been sufficiently proven that they are guilty. If you, however, assume they are guilty and wicked—people who ought not to be spared—you are assuming the very point that is in question. For that is what we were asking: whether a person ought to be considered guilty and wicked...

### Doubt 51. What is the summary of the process against those who proceed against the Clergy without special and specific license from the Apostolic See <term>Apostolicæ sedis</term>? <note>Referring to the authority of the Pope in Rome.</note>

The Inquisitors <term>Inquisitors</term> take care that the most pious Princes, who are most observant of the Roman See, do not understand this, lest they place a bridle <note>original: "fręnum"; a metaphor for legal restraint or control.</note> on these proceedings.

21. Then, when "Gaja" <note>A traditional legal placeholder name for a female defendant, similar to "Jane Doe."</note> has been thus shaken and shaved, she is tortured so that she might "speak the truth"—that is, so that she might pronounce herself simply guilty. Whatever else she might say will not be considered the truth, nor can it be.

22. She is tortured, however, with "torture of the first degree," that is, the lighter kind. Understand it this way: although it is indeed most severe, it is milder only in comparison to the degrees that follow. Hence, if she confesses, the officials say and spread the word that she confessed "without torture." <note>This highlights a common legal loophole: if a prisoner confessed during the "preparation" or the lightest stage of torture, it was recorded as a voluntary confession made without the use of the rack or heavy equipment.</note>

23. Who among the Princes or others who hear this would not believe her to be most certainly guilty, she who thus "voluntarily" confessed her guilt without torture?

24. Therefore, without any hesitation, she is punished after this confession. She would have been punished nonetheless even if she had not confessed; for once the beginning has been given to torture, "the die is cast" <note>original: "jacta alea est"; a reference to an irreversible decision.</note>; she cannot escape, she must die.

### Question 51. What the nature of the proceedings is against...

...[the proof they] gather is always invalid and void, since it is never legitimately proven. 41. Meanwhile, while the trials are so heated, and those who are tortured vigorously denounce others when forced by the most bitter torments; word soon leaks out as to who exactly has been denounced. For this is the nature of "secrecy" among those who assist in the interrogations <term>quaestiones: judicial examinations, almost always involving the use of torture to extract confessions</term>. And this is not without its benefits for them, since they can suddenly seize upon evidence <term>indicia: legal signs or clues that suggested a person's guilt, used to justify further torture</term> against the accused through this dilemma: For if people hear they have been reported—as they surely do—they either flee to avoid being caught, or they remain steadfast in their place. If they take flight, the accusers say this is a huge sign of guilt and a fearful conscience. If they stay, then this too is a sign; for the "demon," they say, holds them back so they cannot leave. As I have lately had to hear, not just once, with a groan of sorrow.

42. Furthermore, if someone approaches the Inquisitors <note>original: "Quaesitores"; officials appointed to lead a criminal inquiry or "quest"</note> and asks if what they have heard is true, so that they might defend themselves in time and use the legal path to meet the approaching trouble, even this is taken as a sign of guilt, as if conscience and blame are driving the person—even though the Inquisitors have not yet taken any action against them.

### Question 51: What is the summary of the process against [witches]?

[...the sum]mary of these times, unless it is provided for otherwise. I have said before, and I repeat it in a word: this plague <term>pestem: referring here to the social and judicial "contagion" of the witch trials</term>, whatever it may be, cannot be abolished by fires <note>original: "incendijs" — a reference to the execution of accused witches by burning at the stake</note>; yet it can be most effectively ended in another way, with hardly any blood being shed. But who will want to know this? It overwhelms me as I try to say more, so that I cannot complete this summary perfectly <note>original: "ad unguem" — literally "to the fingernail," a Latin idiom for finishing a work with absolute precision</note>, nor can I plan a German version <note>original: "versionem Germanicam" — Spee wrote in Latin to reach the educated elite and clergy, but recognizes the need for a vernacular edition for the common people</note>, which otherwise would have been quite useful. Perhaps there will be those who, out of love for their fatherland and for the innocent, will complete it more accurately. 

Finally, I implore all the learned, the pious, the prudent, and the moderate rulers of affairs—for I do not concern myself with the others—by the tribunal of the Almighty Judge, that they diligently examine and weigh what we have written in this treatise. All **Magistrates** and **Princes** are in great danger of losing their salvation <note>meaning their eternal souls</note> unless they choose to be most attentive. Let them not wonder if I occasionally admonish them sharply and spiritedly; for it would not befit me to be among those whom the Prophet calls **"dumb dogs, unable to bark"** <note>original: "canes mutos non valentes latrare" — a reference to Isaiah 56:10, criticizing leaders who fail to warn their people of danger</note>. Let them attend to themselves and to the whole flock, for whom God will one day most strictly demand an accounting from their hands.

## APPENDIX.

### What can torture and denunciations accomplish?

They can do almost everything. Hence, someone recently called torture "Almighty" <note>original: *Omnipotentem*</note> with no small wit. Indeed, many examples are circulated of those who, overcome by torments, confessed the most false things about themselves; some were even executed for the murders of men who were later found to be alive, and other such cases. But I have never wanted to use those examples in this little book—partly so I would not fill the pages with stories (which anyone could do), and partly so that no one would suspect that these cases are rare or do not happen every day. However, I have decided to include one case here that involves a vast multitude of people, and I am surprised it has not been more noted until now; it is as follows:

### A MEMORABLE EXAMPLE.

The City of Rome once burned under the Emperor Nero; whether it happened by accident or by that Prince's command is uncertain; read the historians: Tacitus, Suetonius, Dio, Sulpicius, Baronius, and others. It is cer- <note>The text breaks here at the syllable "Constan-", likely leading into "Constantissimum" or "Constat," meaning "It is well established."</note>

### Appendix.

-tainly <note>original: *certè*</note>, a rumor blamed the Prince <note>Emperor Nero, who ruled from 54 to 68 AD and was famously accused of playing music while Rome burned.</note> for the crime, but he soon shifted this blame onto the Christians. Because common gossip at the time portrayed them as criminals prone to any wickedness, he ordered some to be seized first and tortured. Therefore, overcome by torments, these people confessed about themselves, and then pointed out or denounced others; so that from these denunciations and torments, a vast multitude was suddenly convicted—not only of being guilty of that fire, but even more so for their "hatred of the human race." <note>This "hatred of the human race" (original: *odij in humanū genus*) was a specific Roman legal prejudice against early Christians, who were viewed as antisocial for refusing to participate in the civic and religious life of the Empire.</note>

For this reason, as arsonists and the greatest enemies of the human race, they were punished with various forms of death. Some were covered in the skins of wild beasts and torn to pieces by the mauling of dogs; others were nailed to crosses; others were set on fire, and when the daylight failed, they were burned to serve as lights in the night. This happened because they were fixed to stakes and arranged throughout the amphitheater, then doused in pitch and resin and bound; thus ignited, they blazed like torches. To this, Juvenal <note>A Roman poet known for his biting Satires.</note> alluded when he said in his first *Satire*:

> Describe Tigillinus <note>Sophonius Tigillinus was the powerful and cruel prefect of the Praetorian Guard under Nero, often blamed for the Emperor's worst excesses.</note>; and you will shine in that torch in which they stand and burn, who smoke with their throats fixed to the stake.
> <note>original: *Pone Tigillinum; tæda lucebis in illa / Qua stātes ardēt, qui fixo gutture fumāt.*</note>

The words of Cornelius Tacitus, a trustworthy writer, regarding this entire matter are quite clear in Book 15 of his *Annals*, where he says the following:

### Appendix.

<margin>Dd 2</margin>

Therefore, he [Tacitus] says, to suppress the rumor <note>The rumor that Nero himself had ordered the Great Fire of Rome in 64 AD.</note>, Nero falsely charged and afflicted with the most refined punishments those people whom the common crowd—hating them for their perceived shameful acts—called Christians, etc. Therefore, those who **CONFESSED** <note>original: *FATEBANTUR*; likely referring to confessing their faith or being coerced into confessing to the fire.</note> were seized first. Then, by their **EVIDENCE**, a **VAST MULTITUDE** <note>original: *MULTITUDO INGENS*</note> were **CONVICTED**, not so much for the crime of arson as for their "hatred of the human race." <note>original: *odio humani generis*. In the Roman view, Christians were seen as anti-social and a threat to the state because they refused to participate in traditional civic religious rituals.</note> And mockeries were added to their deaths; they perished covered in the skins of wild beasts, torn apart by dogs, or fastened to crosses, or set ablaze so that when daylight failed, they were burned to serve as light for the night. Thus he [Tacitus] wrote. Regarding this example, let the reader note and consider the following:

**FIRST.** Nero’s legal process against a vast multitude was supported by these indications or proofs: 1. Reputation, by which the Christians were held in very poor regard. 2. Their own confession, wrung out by torments. 3. The denunciations of fellow-confessors; for in this way, innocent men were finally convicted both of arson and of hostility toward the human race.

**SECOND.** **GOD** permitted not just a few to be so convicted and perish, but a vast multitude.

**THIRD.** All those who perished having been so convicted, the Church honors for this very reason as Martyrs, and celebrates their memory on the eighth day before the Kalends of July <note>June 24th. This refers to the "First Martyrs of the Church of Rome" who were killed by Nero.</note>, where it [the liturgy/record] says regarding them:

...speaks the Roman Martyrology <note>The *Martyrologium Romanum* is the official list of martyrs recognized by the Catholic Church, organized by their feast days.</note>.
> *“All these,”* it says, *“were disciples of the Apostles and the first-fruits of the Martyrs <note>original: "primitiæ Martyrum"</note>, whom the Roman Church—that fertile field of Martyrs—sent to the Lord before the death of the Apostles.”*

**FOURTH.** Nor did it hinder their Martyrdom that, overcome by torments, they made both themselves and others "guilty" <note>original: "reos". In a legal context, this means they confessed to the crimes they were accused of, even if those confessions were false and coerced.</note>. For the Martyrology calls all of them, without exception, Martyrs. You will easily understand that the Martyrology is not speaking of one group and Tacitus of another, but plainly of the very same people, if you examine the Martyrology itself, which recites the very words of Tacitus. See also, if you please, the *Annals* of Baronius <note>Caesar Baronius (1538–1607) was an influential Cardinal and historian known for his ecclesiastical history of the Church.</note> for the year of Christ 66, and Sulpitius Severus <note>An early Christian writer (c. 363–425 AD) known for his "Sacred History."</note> in the second book of his *History*.

**FIFTH.** Therefore, neither the Martyrs, nor the **disciples of the Apostles**, nor those struggling in the very first fervor of Christianity, possessed that level of "constancy" <note>An endurance or steadiness of mind.</note> that would prevail against torments and denunciations.

**SIXTH.** This was Nero’s intent in applying torments: that those tortured would confess themselves guilty. Unless that is also the intent of torments today, what, I pray, is intended? Recall what we have said scattered throughout the text above. But if something else is intended, it is a matter for me to rejoice in; it is well.

<header>Appendix</header>

**SEVENTH.** Suppose that judges today intend something different than Nero did; suppose also that they rush to use torture based on more evidence than he did. This, however, does not change the fact that the power of torture is the same now as it was then. Just as torture and denunciations <note>original: "denunciationes" — the act of naming others as accomplices or co-conspirators under pressure.</note> could make even the most innocent person appear guilty <note>original: "reum" — in a legal sense, the person formally accused or the defendant who has been made to look "guilty" by their confession.</note> back then, they can do so now as well. And if those who are denounced today are truly guilty, then those who were denounced back then must also have been truly guilty. Certainly, the mindset of Nero’s judges was not the same as Nero’s own, yet by their judgment, the Martyrs were convicted.

**EIGHTH.** Since Nero, through torture and denunciations, had made a **HUGE MULTITUDE** of even holy men into "criminals," there is no doubt that if he had wished to proceed further, he would never have reached an end to the accused. For just as so many were convicted, the rest could have been convicted as well. This is the very reason today why, when we persist in following these denunciations, it is impossible to reach an end <note>The author is highlighting a "feedback loop": one person under torture names others, who are then tortured and name more, creating an infinite chain of accusations.</note>.

*YOU WILL SAY: Baronius <note>Caesar Baronius (1538–1607), a Catholic historian previously cited.</note> believes that Tacitus <note>The Roman historian (c. 56–120 AD) who provided the earliest non-Christian account of Nero's persecution.</note> is lying in the provided example, regarding the claim that certain Christians, overcome by torture, made themselves and others falsely guilty.*

*RESPONSE: Others, who have a slightly more thorough understanding of the power of torture than many, believe that Tacitus did not*

*...to lie. And indeed, since those Neronian interrogations <note>original: "quaestiones" — in this legal context, these are judicial examinations conducted under torture.</note> were held legally and a sentence was passed, it is not believable that cruelty was used against those who did not confess or who denied the charges; for this would clearly have conflicted with Nero’s intention, since he would have increased the rumors conceived about himself rather than abolishing them. Nor was Tacitus <note>Publius Cornelius Tacitus (c. 56 – c. 120 AD), the Roman historian who provided the primary account of Nero blaming Christians for the Great Fire of Rome.</note> any more unfair to the Christians in this matter than he was to Nero; rather, he favored them, and if you pay attention, he sufficiently hints that the Christians were actually innocent and that Nero was the more guilty party. But Baronius <note>Caesar Baronius (1538–1607), a Catholic cardinal and historian who wrote the "Annales Ecclesiastici."</note> should not wonder that even holy men initially yielded to such exquisite punishments, then later repented and revoked their confessions in vain, yet were nonetheless honored with martyrdom <note>original: "martyrio decoratos" — literally "decorated with martyrdom."</note>. For even today, if the holiest of men were subjected to our judicial examinations, they would succumb just the same; as I have yet to hear of anyone who, having seen these tortures <note>original: "tormenta"</note> from a close distance, continued to maintain their innocence.*

But these things will be clearer one day at the judgment seat of God. Now, farewell Reader; keep this example in your mind, and fear the Divine Power.

### PROTESTATION.

<note>original: "Protestatio" — a standard formal declaration at the end of a work by a Catholic author, submitting their writing to the judgment of the Church to avoid accusations of heresy.</note>

If I have written anything that displeases the Holy Roman Church: let it be void; I condemn and detest it, as well as anything that might unjustly harm anyone. etc.

### THE END.

<summary>The author concludes his historical-legal argument by asserting that even the early Christian martyrs would have broken under torture, just as people do in modern trials. The work ends with a standard submission of the text to the judgment of the Roman Catholic Church.</summary>
